note: Links a describer to a noun, like 's or "of": 我的 wǒ de "my", 好吃的菜 "tasty food". Other readings: dí in 的確 dí què "indeed", dì in 目的 mù dì "goal".
Links two nouns (A 是 B). Not used before adjectives: say 我很累, not 我是累. A bare 是 for "yes" sounds formal; everyday Taiwan speech uses 對 or 嗯.

After a verb it marks a finished action (我吃了 "I ate"); at the end of a sentence it marks a new situation (下雨了 "it's raining now"). Other reading liǎo "to finish", as in 受不了 shòu bu liǎo "can't stand it".
Says where someone or something is (他在家 "he's at home"). Before a verb it means "in the middle of": 我在吃飯 "I'm eating".
Negates habits, wishes and the present/future (我不去 "I'm not going"). Use 沒 for 有 and for things that didn't happen. Spoken bú before a 4th tone: 不要 bú yào.
In speech tā covers he and she. In writing "she" is 她 and "it" is 它/牠, all pronounced tā; in speech "it" is usually left out or said with 這/那.
Negated with 沒 (沒有 "don't have"), never 不有. Taiwan Mandarin also uses 有 before a verb for "did": 我有去 "I did go".
Taiwan uses 我們 for every "we"; the mainland 咱們 ("we, including you") is rarely heard.
Used alone (這是… "this is…") or before a number/measure word (這個, 這次). Before a measure word it is often said zhèi: 這個 zhèi ge.

hint: as soon as; sooner than expected
note: Very flexible adverb: "then / as soon as" (吃完就走 "leave right after eating"), "exactly" (就是他 "it's him"), "only" (就一個 "just one").

example.english: There are so many people here.

note: Joins nouns, not sentences. Many Taiwanese say hàn (an MOE-listed colloquial reading), and in casual speech 跟 is more common. Other readings: hè (附和), huó (和麵), huò, hú (winning in mahjong).

example.pinyin: Bàba hé māma dōu zài jiā.
example.english: Mom and Dad are both home.

note: Added to the end of a statement to make a yes/no question: 你好 → 你好嗎？ Don't use it with question words like 什麼 or 誰.
A learned skill (我會游泳 "I can swim") or what is likely to happen (明天會下雨 "it will rain tomorrow"). Compare 能 (able) and 可以 (allowed). Other reading kuài in 會計 kuài jì "accountant".
Taiwanese often use 講 jiǎng for the same meaning in casual speech. Other reading shuì in 遊說 yóu shuì "to lobby".
Alone it means "okay / sure". Before an adjective it means "so, really" (好累 "so tired"), very common in Taiwan. Other reading hào "to be fond of" (愛好 ài hào).

gloss: to want; to need to; will
note: More direct than 想. Also "need to / should" (你要小心 "be careful") and "about to" (要下雨了). Other reading yāo in 要求 yāo qiú "to demand".

example.english: What would you like to drink?

note: Goes before the verb and sums up the people or things already mentioned: 我們都去 "we're all going". Other reading dū "capital city" (首都 shǒu dū).
Goes before the verb, never at the end: 我也是 "me too".
In fast Taiwan speech it often sounds like shé me.
Also "let me / I'll do it" before a verb (我來 "let me"), and after verbs for movement toward the speaker (拿來 "bring here").
Alone it means "yes, right". As a preposition it means "to / toward": 他對我很好 "he's good to me". Also counts pairs: 一對 "a pair".
Tone changes in speech: yí before a 4th tone (一個 yí ge), yì before other tones (一起 yì qǐ), yī when counting or at the end.
Often just links a subject and an adjective without much "very": 我很好 "I'm fine".
The default measure word, used for people and most things that lack a special one: 一個人, 兩個問題. Usually unstressed in speech (ge).
Also "to (a place)" (到台北 "to Taipei") and "until" (到明天). After a verb it means you succeeded: 找到 "found", 看到 "saw".
A place word: 桌上 "on the table". As a verb "to go up / get on / attend": 上車 "get in the car", 上班 "go to work". Also "last": 上個月 "last month".

example.english: The phone is on the bed.

hint: one syllable; able to, circumstances allow
note: Ability or possibility in the situation. In Taiwan it is heard most in the negative (不能 "can't"); for requests people usually say 可以. Compare 會 (learned skill) and 可以 (permission).
In writing also 她們 (female) and 它們 (things); all are pronounced tā men.
"Still" (還在 "still here"), "yet" with 沒 (還沒 "not yet"), "in addition" (還要 "want more"). Other reading huán "to give back" (還錢 huán qián).

gloss: to want to; to think; to miss
note: Before a verb it is a softer "want to" than 要. Before a person it means "to miss": 我想你 "I miss you".
Negates 有 ("don't have, there isn't") and past actions (我沒有去 "I didn't go"). Often shortened to 沒. Also a common short answer: "No."
Before a measure word often said nèi (那個 nèi ge). At the start of a sentence it means "then / so": 那我們走吧 "then let's go". The "which" question word is written 哪 nǎ.
Makes a suggestion (走吧 "let's go") or asks for agreement (你是老師吧？ "you're a teacher, right?"). Other reading bā in 酒吧 jiǔ bā "bar".
Knowing a fact or information. Compare 認識 (to know a person) and 會 (know how to). MOE lists both zhī dao and zhī dào; Taiwan speakers usually keep the 4th tone on dào.
讓 + person + verb: "let/make someone do": 讓他很生氣 "made him angry". Also "to give way" (讓位 "give up your seat").

example.english: Let me think for a sec.

note: Short for 沒有: negates 有 and things that didn't happen; use 不 for habits and the future. Other reading mò "to sink" (沒收 mò shōu "confiscate").
把 + thing + verb: "take X and do something to it": 把門關上 "close the door". Also a measure word for things with handles: 一把傘 "an umbrella", 一把鑰匙 "a key".
Also "for / to" before a person: 打給我 "call me", 給你看 "let you see". Other reading jǐ in 供給 gōng jǐ "supply". Compare 送 (to give as a gift).
After a verb it marks a continuing state: 門開著 "the door is open", 坐著 "sitting". Other readings: zháo in 睡著 shuì zháo "fall asleep", zhù in 著名 zhù míng "famous", zhuó in 著陸 "land".

hint: two syllables; this one, with a measure word
note: Very often said zhèi ge. Also used as a filler, like "um", while thinking.
Same sound as 作 zuò in 工作 "work".
Asks or gives permission. As a reply it means "sure / that works" or "not bad". Compare 會 (learned skill) and 能 (able).
Mostly heard in 為什麼 "why" and 為了 "in order to". Other reading wéi "to act as / be", in 認為 rèn wéi "to think" and 成為 chéng wéi "to become".

gloss: to look; to watch; to read
note: Also "to visit / see" (看醫生 "see a doctor") and "it depends" (看你 "up to you"). Other reading kān "to look after" (看家 kān jiā).

example.english: Do you want to watch a movie?

note: After a verb it means "have ever done": 去過 "have been". As a verb: "to cross / pass / spend (time)": 過馬路, 過年. MOE gives guò; the mainland says unstressed guo for the "ever" meaning.
Marks the passive, usually for something bad: 被罵 "got scolded". Also means "quilt" in 棉被 mián bèi. Other reading pī (literary).

example.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le.

note: Ends a sentence to add feeling or soften it: 好啊 'sure!', 是啊 'yeah'. Its sound blends with the word before: after -a/-e/-i/-o/-ü it sounds like ya (呀), after -u/-ao/-ou like wa (哇), so 好啊 is heard as hǎo wa, and after -n like na (哪); said alone, ā or á means 'ah!' or 'huh?'.

gloss: (links a verb to how / how well)
note: Goes after a verb or adjective to say how or how well: 說得很好 'speaks well', 聽得懂 'can understand (by listening)'. Other readings: dé 'to get' (得到 dé dào) and děi 'must' (我得走了 wǒ děi zǒu le). Sounds the same as 的 and 地.

example.pinyin: Nǐ Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.

note: Short, slightly more formal form of 但是. In everyday speech 但是 or 可是 kě shì is more common.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qù, dàn méiyǒu shíjiān.
example.english: I want to go, but I don't have time.

note: Before a verb it asks how to do something: 怎麼用？ 'how do you use it?'. Before a situation it asks 'how come', often surprised: 你怎麼來了？ 'how come you're here?'.

hint: one syllable, not 'inside'; after a verb: in progress
note: After a verb it can mean 'in progress', common on Taiwan signs and in speech: 營業中 'open', 考慮中 'thinking it over'. Other reading zhòng 'to hit; to win', as in 中獎 zhòng jiǎng 'win a prize'.
Counted directly, with no measure word: 三年 sān nián 'three years'. 今年 'this year', 明年 'next year', 去年 'last year'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zài Táiwān zhù le sān nián.
example.english: I lived in Taiwan for three years.
It's fine, I'll do it myself.

hint: one syllable; an affair, not an object
note: Very common in 沒事 méi shì 'it's nothing / I'm fine' and 有事 yǒu shì 'I'm busy / something's up'. A physical thing is 東西. Taiwan does not use the mainland erhua 事兒.
Often paired with 就 jiù in the second half: 如果下雨，我就不去 'if it rains, I won't go'.

example.pinyin: Rúguǒ nǐ lèi le, jiù zǎo diǎn shuì.
example.english: If you're tired, go to bed early.

hint: one syllable, after a place or thing
note: Goes after a noun to mean 'in': 家裡 jiā lǐ 'at home', 包包裡 'in the bag'. Standing alone, 'inside' is 裡面 lǐ miàn.

example.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī zài bāobāo lǐ.
example.english: My phone is in my bag.

note: Also 'how' in questions: 多大 'how old/big', 多久 'how long'; and 'more than' after numbers: 二十多 'twenty-something'. For the 'how' sense MOE gives duó, but most speakers say duō.

example.english: There are so many people today!

note: Often paired with 所以 suǒ yǐ 'so': 因為下雨，所以我沒去 'because it rained, I didn't go'.

example.english: We didn't go out because it rained.

note: Marks where or when something starts: 從台北來 'come from Taipei', 從明天開始 'starting tomorrow'. Often paired with 到: 從早到晚 'from morning to night'. MOE also lists rare literary readings (zòng, cōng, zōng).

example.pinyin: Wǒ shì cóng Táiběi lái de.

note: A somewhat formal connector. In speech it mostly appears in set patterns: 不是…而是… 'not … but rather …', 而且 'moreover', 而已 'that's all'.

example.english: The problem isn't money, it's time.

note: Describes a way or a situation: 這樣做 'do it this way', 是這樣 'it's like this'. Before an adjective ('this big'), 這麼 is more usual. Taiwan speakers often say zhèi yàng.
Goes before the verb: 我只要一個 'I only want one'. 只有 'only (have)' and 只是 'just; merely' are common. Other reading zhī is the measure word for animals, written 隻 in Traditional.
Counts animals (一隻狗 'a dog', 兩隻貓 'two cats') and one of a pair (一隻手 'one hand'). Different tone from 只 zhǐ 'only'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu liǎng zhī māo.
example.english: We have two cats at home.

note: Also 'older' for age: 他比我大兩歲 'he's two years older than me'. Other reading dài only in 大夫 dài fu 'doctor' (old-fashioned).

gloss: down; below; next; to get off
note: Opposite of 上: 下車 'get off (a vehicle)', 下雨 'to rain', 下班 'get off work', 下次 'next time'. After a verb it means 'down' (坐下 'sit down'); 一下 makes a request softer.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zài xià yī zhàn xiàchē.
example.english: I'm getting off at the next stop.

note: Also means 'with/using': 用手吃 'eat with your hands'. 不用 bù yòng means 'no need'.
Usually comes with 了 le at the end: 他已經走了 'he's already left'.
等一下 means 'wait a moment' or 'in a moment'. 等…再… means 'once …, then …': 等你到了再說 'we'll talk when you get here'. In writing it can also mean 'etc.'

example.pinyin: Děng wǒ yīxià, wǒ mǎshàng lái!
example.english: Wait a second, I'll be right there!

note: Asks 'what about …?' (你呢？ 'and you?'), softens a question (怎麼辦呢？ 'what should we do?'), or marks an ongoing state (他在睡覺呢 'he's sleeping'). Other reading ní only in 呢絨 'wool fabric'.

hint: one syllable; 'a bit' after an adjective
note: Tells the time: 三點 'three o'clock', 幾點？ 'what time?'. 一點 means 'a little'. As a verb it means 'to order' (點菜) or 'to light' (點火). Taiwan says 一點, not mainland erhua 一點兒.
Taiwan says 這裡 or 這邊 zhè biān for 'here', not the mainland erhua 這兒 zhèr.
Goes before an adjective or verb: 最好 'best', 最喜歡 'like the most', 最近 'lately'.
'Again' for something that hasn't happened yet (再說一次 'say it again'); 又 yòu is for a repeat that already happened. Also 'then, after that': 吃完再走 'eat first, then go'. Same sound as 在 zài 'at'.

hint: literally 'true'; one syllable, before an adjective
note: Before an adjective it means 'really, so': 真好 'so nice', 真可愛 'so cute'. On its own, 'really?' is 真的 zhēn de.

example.english: The weather is really nice today!

note: Very common in Taiwan for 'with/and' (instead of 和): 我跟你去 'I'll go with you'. Also 'to' after talking verbs (跟他說 'tell him') and the verb 'to follow'.

hint: one syllable; mostly in set phrases
note: Mostly heard inside 可以 'can', 可是 'but', 可能 and 可愛, and in the question 可不可以 'can I?' (a shortened 可以不可以). Before a verb it can add emphasis (你可要小心喔 'you'd better be careful'); other reading kè only in 可汗 'khan'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ kě bù kěyǐ zuò zhèlǐ?

note: 沒問題 méi wèn tí 'no problem' is a very common reply.

example.trad: 我可以問你一個問題嗎？
example.simp: 我可以问你一个问题吗？
example.pinyin: Wǒ kěyǐ wèn nǐ yī ge wèntí ma?
example.english: Can I ask you a question?

note: 'Again' for a repeat that already happened: 他又遲到了 'he's late again' (for the future use 再 zài). 又…又… means 'both … and …': 又便宜又好吃 'cheap and tasty'.
Mostly in …的時候 'when …' (我小的時候 'when I was little') and 什麼時候 'when?'. Time as an amount is 時間. Taiwan says shí hòu; the mainland usually says shí hou.
Spoken shéi; shuí is the formal reading pronunciation, also heard in songs.

example.pinyin: Nǐ zài gēn shéi jiǎng diànhuà?
example.english: Who are you on the phone with?

hint: two syllables, the firmer 'but'; not kě shì
note: Standard 'but'; 可是 kě shì is softer and very common in speech. MOE lists a neutral-tone dàn shi, but Taiwanese speakers usually say dàn shì.

example.trad: 我很想去，但是我太累了。
example.simp: 我很想去，但是我太累了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xiǎng qù, dànshì wǒ tài lèi le.
example.english: I really want to go, but I'm too tired.

note: Taiwan speakers often say zhèi xiē.
快…了 means 'almost, about to': 快到了 'almost there'. 快一點 'hurry up'.

example.pinyin: Kuài yīdiǎn, wǒmen yào chídào le!
example.english: Hurry up, we're going to be late!

note: In speech it often means 'to leave': 他走了 'he left', 我們走吧 'let's go'. Going to a place is usually 去 qù.

example.pinyin: Shíjiān bù zǎo le, wǒmen zǒu ba.

gloss: to go out; to come out; out
note: Often in compounds and after verbs: 出門 'leave the house', 出去 'go out', 拿出來 'take out'.
Mostly in set words: 以後 'after; later', 後面 'behind', 最後 'finally'. On its own it follows an event: 下班後 'after work'.

hint: too much; or 'so …!' with le at the end
note: 太…了 means 'too …' or, for good things, 'so …!': 太好了 'great!'. 不太 means 'not very': 不太好 'not so good'.

hint: one syllable; 'even more', before an adjective
note: Goes before an adjective or verb: 更好 'even better'. Other reading gēng means 'to change', as in 更新 gēng xīn 'to update'.

example.english: Today is even colder than yesterday.

note: Here 為 is wèi 'for'; in 因為 it is also wèi, but in 成為 'to become' and 以為 'to think (wrongly)' it is wéi.
The everyday way to give an opinion, softer than 認為 rèn wéi. 覺 is read jiào in 睡覺 shuì jiào 'to sleep'.
聽到 or 聽見 means 'to hear (something)'; 聽得懂 means 'can understand by listening'. MOE also lists a rare literary reading tìng 'to allow'.
Added to pronouns and people nouns: 我們 (wǒ men) 'we', 你們 'you all', 朋友們 'friends'. Not used for things. MOE gives mén as the reading form, but in speech it is always the light men.
Short, everyday form of 應該 'should'. Very common in 該走了 (gāi zǒu le) 'time to go' and 該你了 'your turn'.
Often in 像…一樣 'just like…'. 好像 (hǎo xiàng) means 'it seems'.

example.pinyin: Tā zhǎng de hěn xiàng tā bàba.
example.english: He looks a lot like his dad.

gloss: exactly; that's it; it's just that
note: 就 adds emphasis to 是: 'is exactly'. Alone, 就是！ means 'Exactly!'. 就是說 'that is to say'; 就是…而已 'it's just…'.
Before an adjective it means 'so': 這麼貴 (zhè me guì) 'so expensive'. Before a verb, 'like this': 這麼做 'do it this way'. Compare 那麼 'that much / like that'.

example.english: Why is it so hot today?

note: Taiwan says xǐ huān with a full first tone on 歡; mainland speech usually has a light xǐ huan. Followed by a noun or a verb: 喜歡吃辣 'like eating spicy food'.

example.english: What do you like to eat?

note: Mostly placed before 不 or 沒 to stress 'actually not, contrary to what you think': 並不難 (bìng bù nán) 'not hard at all'. In formal speech it also means 'and also'.

gloss: only then; not until; only (so few)
note: Means 'not until' (十點才來 'didn't come until ten'), 'just now' (我才到 'I just got here') or 'only' (才三個 'only three'). The opposite feel of 就, which means 'already, as early as'.

example.english: He didn't get up until ten.

note: Also used to guess: 他應該到了 'he's probably arrived'. 該 (gāi) is the short form.

example.english: You should go to bed earlier.

note: Both the noun 'job' (找工作 'look for a job') and the verb 'to work'. 上班 (shàng bān) is 'to go to work / be at work'.
For amounts use 少 (shǎo) 'few, little'. 小 before a surname is a friendly nickname: 小王 'Little Wang'.
Time as an amount or free time (有時間嗎 'do you have time?'). For 'when / the time that…', use 時候 (shí hòu).
Before an adjective it means 'that': 沒那麼難 'not that hard'. At the start of a sentence it means 'well then, in that case' (often shortened to 那 nà).

hint: one syllable; telling someone not to
note: 別 + verb is a command, same as 不要: 別走 'don't go', 別擔心 'don't worry'. Also 'other' in 別人 'other people' and 別的 'something else'.
The everyday Taiwan 'excuse me / sorry' for small things: getting someone's attention, bumping into someone, asking a favor. It also means 'to feel embarrassed'. 對不起 is for real apologies.

example.trad: 不好意思，請問廁所在哪裡？
example.simp: 不好意思，请问厕所在哪里？

hint: as a result; the everyday word
note: Introduces a result, often paired with 因為: 因為…所以… 'because…, so…'. Also a conversational filler 'so…'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn lèi, suǒyǐ xiān shuì le.
example.english: I'm tired, so I'm going to bed first.

note: Counts days with no measure word: 三天 (sān tiān) 'three days'. Also in 今天 'today', 天氣 'weather' and 天啊 'oh my god'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ děng le nǐ yī zhěng tiān.
example.english: I waited for you all day.

note: Adds something ('also, and another thing') or says something remains: 還有時間 'there's still time'. 還 is hái here; it is huán in 還錢 'pay back money'.
MOE gives the light gào su for 'to tell'; many Taiwanese say gào sù with a full fourth tone. Followed by the person: 告訴我 'tell me'. Compare 說 'to say'.
Stronger than 喜歡 'to like'. Before a verb it means 'love to, tend to': 他很愛哭 'he cries a lot'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn ài wǒ de jiārén.

gloss: to be (a role); to work as; when
hint: take on a role or job
note: 當 + role means 'to be, work as': 當老師 'be a teacher'. 當…的時候 means 'when…'. Read dàng in 當作 (dàng zuò) 'treat as' and 上當 'get fooled'.

example.english: I want to be a teacher someday.

gloss: to get up; to rise; (after verb) up
note: Alone: 'get up'. After a verb: upward (站起來 'stand up'), starting (笑起來 'start laughing'), or an impression (看起來 'looks', 聽起來 'sounds'). Taiwan keeps the full lái; after a verb it is often said lightly.

example.english: Get up, you're going to be late!

note: Month names are numbered: 一月 'January', 三月 'March'. For 'a month' as a length of time, add 個: 一個月 'one month'. The moon itself is usually 月亮.
After an adjective it means 'to death, extremely': 熱死了 'it's boiling', 累死了 'I'm exhausted'.
說話 'to talk', 電話 'phone', 笑話 'joke'. At the end of a clause, 的話 means 'if': 下雨的話 'if it rains'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ shuō de huà wǒ tīngbudǒng.
example.english: I don't understand what you're saying.

hint: one syllable; after a time, as in "three days ago"
note: After a time it means 'ago': 三天前 'three days ago'. Also in 前面 'in front' and 以前 'before, in the past'.

example.pinyin: Tā sān tiān qián jiù huílai le.
example.english: He already came back three days ago.

hint: a considered opinion; more formal than jué de
note: For giving an opinion, a bit more serious than 覺得 (jué de). 為 is wéi here (as in 以為 'mistakenly think') but wèi in 為什麼 'why'.

example.english: I think this way is better.

note: Used before measure words: 兩個人 'two people', 兩天 'two days'. Use 二 (èr) when counting and in numbers (一、二、三; 十二). Also an old weight unit, the tael.
找到 means 'to find (successfully)'. 找你 means 'to come see you'. At a shop, 找錢 means 'to give change'.
MOE gives the light dōng xi for 'thing'; many Taiwanese say dōng xī with a full tone, which is also the reading for 'east and west'.
請坐 'please sit'. 請問 'excuse me, may I ask'. Also 'to treat': 我請你 'it's on me'. 請假 means 'to take time off'.
As a reply it means 'oh, I see' (often ò or ó when surprised). At the end of a sentence it is light (o) and adds a friendly reminder tone: 小心喔 'be careful, OK?', 好喔 'OK!'. Very Taiwanese.
Also the go-to filler while thinking: 那個… 'um…'. Often said nèi ge. MOE also lists nǎ ge, an old form of 哪個 'which one'.

example.english: I want that one, not this one.

note: The usual reply to 對不起 or 不好意思. MOE gives a light last syllable here, though 關係 alone is guān xì; many Taiwanese say méi guān xì.

example.english: It's fine, I'll wait for you.

note: In everyday Taiwan speech, 小孩 (xiǎo hái) is just as common.
地上 'on the ground/floor', 地方 'place'. As an adverb particle it is read de (慢慢地 'slowly') and sounds the same as 的.

hint: casual; mostly in "what are you doing?" or "why?"
note: Safe everyday uses: 幹嘛 (gàn má) 'what are you doing / why', 能幹 'capable'. Caution: in Taiwan 幹！ on its own is a strong swear word (like 'f***').

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ de xīn shǒujī.

note: Goes before the verb: 一起吃飯 'eat together'. 在一起 also means 'to be (a couple) together'.
Usually 所有的 + noun, with 都 before the verb: 所有的人都… 'everyone…'. Compare 都 'all' (adverb) and 全部 'the whole lot'.

example.pinyin: Suǒyǒu de rén dōu lái le.

hint: everyday word, as in "same as you"
note: 跟…一樣 'the same as…'; 不一樣 'different'. 像…一樣 'just like…'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ de xiǎngfǎ gēn nǐ yīyàng.
example.english: I think the same as you.

note: Counts occurrences: 一次 'once', 兩次 'twice', 下次 'next time', 第一次 'the first time'.
多少錢？ 'How much?'. 有錢 'rich'. 找錢 'give change'.

gloss: to bring; to take along; to carry
note: 帶你去 'take you there', 帶小孩 'look after kids'. As a noun: belt, band, area (這一帶 'around here'). The Taiwan-style 有帶 means 'did bring'.

gloss: to be called; to call; to tell (sb to)
note: 你叫什麼名字？ 'What's your name?'. 叫他來 'tell him to come'. 叫車 'call a cab'. For a phone call, use 打電話.

Also 'part, aspect': 有些地方我不懂 'there are parts I don't get'. Taiwan and MOE use the full dì fāng for 'place / part'; MOE's light dì fang is only an old word for a village constable. Mainland speech usually says dì fang.
The thing that happens comes after the verb: 發生什麼事？ 'what happened?'.

example.english: I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.

gloss: to hit; to call (phone); to play
note: A very general verb: 打電話 'make a call', 打球 'play ball', 打電動 'play video games' (Taiwan), 打工 'part-time job'. Read dá only for 'dozen' (一打).

example.pinyin: Wǒ děng yīxià dǎ gěi nǐ.
example.english: I'll call you in a bit.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen jiā yǒu sān zhī māo.
example.english: We have three cats at home.

note: Also used for medicine: 吃藥 'take medicine'. In Taiwan, 口吃 'to stutter' is read kǒu jí.
看 is 'to look, watch'; 看到 adds the result, 'actually saw'. 沒看到 'didn't see'. Taiwan often says 有看到 'did see'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yǒu kàndào wǒ de shǒujī ma?

note: Means the same as 這裡 zhè lǐ and is very common in Taiwan: 來這邊 lái zhè biān 'come over here'. Also 'our end, where we are': 我們這邊 wǒ men zhè biān. Its pair is 那邊 nà biān 'over there'. Before a measure word or in fast speech it is often zhèi biān.

example.english: It's not raining where we are.

note: In Taiwan, 我先生 is the usual polite way to say 'my husband'. Taiwan says xiān shēng with a full tone; mainland dictionaries give xiān sheng.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiānshēng jīntiān bù zài jiā.

note: Marks a direction or the person an action is aimed at: 向他道歉 (apologize to him). For physical movement, 往 is more common, and in casual speech 跟 often replaces it.

hint: one syllable; as in 'see you tomorrow'
note: Alone it mostly appears in set phrases like 再見 (bye) and 明天見 (see you tomorrow); for 'to see' people usually say 看到. An old reading, xiàn, means 'to appear' (now written 現).
Also a measure word for shops, restaurants and companies: 一家店 (yī jiā diàn, a shop). An old reading, gū, is not used in everyday speech.

gloss: to open; to drive; to turn on
note: Covers many things: 開門 (open the door), 開車 (drive a car), 開燈 (turn on the light), 開會 (have a meeting).
Comparison pattern: A 比 B + adjective, e.g. 他比我高 (he is taller than me). Never add 很 before the adjective. The readings bì and pí are literary and rare.

example.english: My older brother is a bit taller than me.

note: A softer, more casual 'but' than 但是. Also means 'only, merely': 不過是個小問題 (it's only a small problem). 不 is spoken bú before the 4th tone.

example.english: It's tasty, but a bit expensive.

note: Links steps in order: 先…然後… (first…, then…). Taiwanese speakers also use it constantly as a filler while telling a story, like 'and then…'.

example.trad: 我們先吃飯，然後去看電影。
example.simp: 我们先吃饭，然后去看电影。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen xiān chīfàn, ránhòu qù kàn diànyǐng.
example.english: Let's eat first, then go see a movie.

note: MOE gives péng yǒu with a full tone; mainland dictionaries give péng you (neutral). Both are heard in Taiwan. 男朋友 / 女朋友 = boyfriend / girlfriend.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ de hǎo péngyǒu.

note: Stronger than 很. In casual Taiwan speech 超 or 好 are also common: 超好吃 (super tasty).
The second syllable is neutral in the dictionary, though many Taiwanese say it with two full 4th tones. 感謝 is the more formal 'to thank'.
Something keeps happening or has been true all along: 他一直哭 (he keeps crying). Also 'straight ahead': 一直走 (go straight). 一 is spoken yì here.

example.english: I've always wanted to go to Japan.

note: Stronger and a bit more formal than 要 or 得 (děi). The negative is 不用 or 不必 ('don't have to'), not 不必須.

example.english: I have to get up early tomorrow.
I noticed my phone was gone.

note: In questions 'A 還是 B?' means 'A or B?' (in statements use 或是/或者). Also 'still' and 'had better': 你還是去吧 (you'd better go). 還 here is hái, not huán; Taiwan says shì with a full tone, mainland often hái shi.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yào hē kāfēi háishì chá?
example.english: Do you want coffee or tea?

note: Taiwan says 哪裡 (or 哪邊) where the mainland often says 哪兒. Also a modest reply to a compliment: 哪裡哪裡 (oh, not at all). Spoken ná lǐ (tone sandhi).
Plural of 那 (that). Often pronounced nèi xiē in speech. MOE also lists an old reading nǎ xiē ('which ones'), now written 哪些.

gloss: wait a moment; in a bit; later
note: Two everyday uses: 'hold on!' and 'in a little while, later' (我等一下打給你 wǒ děng yī xià dǎ gěi nǐ 'I'll call you in a bit'). Spoken děng yí xià (一 changes before a 4th tone). 等等 děng děng is a shorter 'wait'.

example.english: I'm heading out in a bit.

gloss: to take; to hold; to get
note: Picking up, holding or fetching something by hand: 拿出來 (take out), 拿走 (take away). 帶 is 'to bring along' with you.

example.pinyin: Kěyǐ bāng wǒ ná shuǐ ma?
example.english: Could you get me some water?

note: Introduces a purpose or beneficiary: 為了你 (for you), 為了省錢 (to save money). 為 here is wèi (for), not wéi (to be).

example.pinyin: Wǒ zuò zhèxiē dōu shì wèile nǐ.
example.english: I did all this for you.

note: 'Just, only': 我只是問問 (I'm only asking). At the start of a clause it is a mild 'but': 我想去，只是沒時間 (I'd like to go, it's just that I have no time).
As a command, 'don't': 不要哭 (don't cry); 別 is a shorter equivalent. Also simply 'not want': 我不要 (I don't want it). 不 is spoken bú before 要.
Certainty or insistence: 他一定會來 (he'll definitely come), 你一定要來 (you must come). 不一定 = not necessarily. 一 is spoken yí here.
After another verb it shows coming out or becoming clear, usually with a light tone: 拿出來 (take out), 看出來 (figure out). 出去 is 'to go out' (away from the speaker).

hint: two syllables; an affair, not an object
note: A matter or something to deal with, never a physical object (that is 東西). MOE gives shì qíng with a full tone; mainland dictionaries give shì qing.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu shìqíng yào gēn nǐ shuō.
example.english: I have something to tell you.

note: Rarely used alone; mostly in 起床 (get out of bed), 一起 (together), 對不起 (sorry), 從今天起 (starting today) and 買不起 (can't afford).

example.english: I get up at six every day.

note: Everyday life and living conditions. 生命 is life as opposed to death; 人生 is one's life journey.

example.english: Life in Taipei is very convenient.

note: After a verb it makes the action brief or softens a request: 等一下 (wait a moment), 看一下 (take a look). 一 is spoken yí here.
An unspecified amount, before a noun: 一些錢 (some money), 一些人 (some people). 有些 is 'some (but not others)', and 幾 'a few' needs a measure word. 一 is spoken yì here.
Also 'to reply': 回訊息 (reply to a message). As a measure word it counts occurrences (兩回事, two different things), though 次 is more common for 'times'.

example.english: What time are you coming home?

note: Asking a question. To ask someone to do something is 請 or 叫; to ask for something is 要.

example.trad: 我可以問你一個問題嗎？
example.simp: 我可以问你一个问题吗？
example.pinyin: Wǒ kěyǐ wèn nǐ yī ge wèntí ma?
example.english: Can I ask you a question?

note: Adds a further point, often paired with 不但 or 不只: 不但便宜，而且好吃 (not only cheap, but also tasty).

example.trad: 這家店很便宜，而且很好吃。
example.simp: 这家店很便宜，而且很好吃。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn hěn piányi, érqiě hěn hǎochī.
example.english: This place is cheap, and the food is good too.

note: An adverb, so it goes after the subject: 他很累，卻睡不著. It sounds a bit more bookish than 可是 or 但是.

example.english: He's tired, yet he can't fall asleep.

example.trad: 這是世界上最好吃的麵！
example.simp: 这是世界上最好吃的面！
example.pinyin: Zhè shì shìjiè shàng zuì hǎochī de miàn!
example.english: These are the best noodles in the world!

note: 這 (this) + 種 (kind, type). Goes before a noun: 這種人 (this kind of person). Often pronounced zhèi zhǒng in speech.

example.english: I don't like this kind of weather.

note: The others or the rest of a group: 其他人 (everyone else). 別的 is the more casual 'other, else'.

'OK, will do' or 'capable': 你真行 (you're really good). 不行 (no way, not OK) is very common in Taiwan, while a plain 'OK' is more often 可以 or 好. Read háng for 'row' or 'business', as in 銀行 (yín háng, bank).
Read hào chī it means 'greedy for food'. For drinks, use 好喝 hǎo hē.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn de miàn hěn hǎochī.
example.english: The noodles at this place are really good.

note: 'Everything' as a whole, slightly formal; casual speech often uses 全部 or 什麼都. 一 is spoken yí here.
Usually followed by a measure word or noun: 哪個 (which one), 哪天 (which day). Often pronounced něi in speech, and as a sentence-final particle it is na.
去公司 (go to the company) is the everyday way to say 'go to work / the office'.

hint: believe a person or what they say
note: 相 here is xiāng (mutual), not xiàng (photo, appearance).

example.english: I believe you can do it.

note: A small amount (一點水, a little water), or after an adjective 'a bit more': 快一點 (a bit faster). Taiwan says 一點 or 一點點 where the mainland says 一點兒. Also 'one o'clock'. 一 is spoken yì here.

hint: one syllable; right then, just about to
note: As an adverb it marks an action in progress or about to happen: 我正要出門 (I'm just about to go out). Also 'straight, upright, correct'. Read zhēng in 正月 (first lunar month).

example.pinyin: Wǒ zhèng yào dǎ gěi nǐ.
example.english: I was just about to call you.

note: Taiwan says 那裡 or 那邊 where the mainland often says 那兒, and keeps a full tone on lǐ. MOE also lists an old reading nǎ lǐ meaning 'where' (now written 哪裡).
After a verb it means 'wrongly': 說錯 (say it wrong), 打錯了 (wrong number). 不錯 means 'pretty good'. MOE also lists a literary reading cù.

hint: all of us / you all, as a group
note: Everyone in the group being talked to or about: 大家好 (hi everyone). The rare reading dà gū is an old word for mother-in-law.
In Taiwan, 殺價 (shā jià) is the everyday word for haggling over a price.

example.english: I can't bring myself to kill a fish.

note: Close to 覺得 jué de 'to think/feel'; 感覺 leans more toward physical or gut feelings and also works as a noun.

hint: become (a role or status), a bit formal
note: A bit more formal than 變成 biàn chéng. For jobs, everyday speech uses 當 dāng (當老師 'be a teacher'). 為 here is wéi, not wèi.
Used for dates (五月三號 'May 3rd'), room or bus numbers, and sizes. Other reading háo 'to howl' is rare.

hint: any at all, before a noun
note: Comes before a noun and is usually followed by 都 or 也: 任何人都可以 'anyone can'.

example.trad: 你有任何問題都可以問我。
example.simp: 你有任何问题都可以问我。
example.pinyin: Nǐ yǒu rènhé wèntí dōu kěyǐ wèn wǒ.
example.english: If you have any questions, you can ask me.

gloss: to help; to do for someone
note: 幫 takes the person right after it and often means 'do something for': 幫我拿 'get it for me'. Compare 幫忙 bāng máng 'to help out' (no object) and 幫助 bāng zhù (more formal).

example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ bāng wǒ yīxià ma?
example.english: Can you help me for a second?

note: Also 'the last': 最後一個 'the last one'. Not the relieved 'finally, at last', which is 終於 zhōng yú.

example.english: In the end he came after all.

note: Polyphone: zhǎng means 'to grow' or 'chief', as in 長大 zhǎng dà 'grow up' and 長得很漂亮 zhǎng de 'looks pretty'. For a long time, use 久 jiǔ.

hint: a plan; verb use is formal
note: Taiwan's standard spelling is 計畫; mainland China writes 計劃 (计划). The pronunciation is the same.

example.english: Do you have any plans for the weekend?

note: Other readings: lěi 'to accumulate' (累積 lěi jī) and léi in 累贅 léi zhuì 'a burden'.
Short for 或者 / 或是, used in statements. In questions ('A or B?') use 還是 hái shì instead.

example.pinyin: Hē chá huò kāfēi dōu kěyǐ.
example.english: Tea or coffee, either is fine.

note: Differs from 賣 mài 'to sell' only by tone: 3rd tone buys, 4th tone sells.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng mǎi xīn de shǒujī.
example.english: I want to buy a new phone.

note: 不能 means unable or not permitted; 不會 means don't know how or won't; 不可以 is mostly 'not allowed'.

example.english: Which countries have you been to?

note: Often paired with direction words: 進來 'come in', 進去 'go in'. 請進 is 'please come in'.
The polite 'you' for elders, customers and strangers. Taiwan uses it less in casual talk than Beijing does; it is common in shops and service settings.

example.english: May I ask your last name?

note: The short form 媽 (我媽 'my mom') is counted here. 母親 mǔ qīn is the formal word.

example.pinyin: Wǒ māma hěn huì zuò cài.
example.english: My mom is a great cook.

note: 重 is zhòng here ('heavy, important'); it is chóng in 重新 chóng xīn 'again'.

hint: two syllables; 'very many', before a noun
note: 很 + 多. This is the normal way to say 'many' before a noun (很多人 'lots of people'); 多 alone rarely goes before a noun.

example.english: I have a lot of friends.

note: Common in 開車 'to drive' and 坐車 'to ride (in a vehicle)'. Other reading jū (the chariot piece in Chinese chess) is rare.
打電話 means 'to make a phone call'.

example.pinyin: Děng yīxià dǎ diànhuà gěi wǒ.
example.english: Give me a call in a bit.

hint: see clearly; it's clear to me
note: MOE gives a neutral second syllable, but many Taiwanese say míng bái with a full tone. In casual Taiwan speech, 懂 dǒng is also very common.
After another verb it means 'firmly, in place': 記住 'remember', 抓住 'grab hold of'.
More formal than 怎麼 / 怎麼樣, but common in speech in 你覺得如何？ 'what do you think?'.

example.english: What do you think of doing it this way?

hint: soft guess; adverb only, not formal
note: Close to 可能 kě néng, which is more common in everyday Taiwan speech.

example.pinyin: Yěxǔ tā jīntiān bù lái le.

note: Takes the place or person left as an object (離開台灣). 走 zǒu is the casual 'to leave, go'.
Other reading xiè appears only in a few literary words.

example.english: How do you write your name?

gloss: how is it?; how about it?
hint: three syllables, the full everyday form
note: Asks for an opinion or condition: 最近怎麼樣？ 'how have you been?'. 不怎麼樣 means 'not great'.

A very common Taiwan answer to 'how was it?': 還好 'it was OK' (often meaning 'nothing special'). At the start of a sentence it means 'luckily, good thing': 還好你來了 hái hǎo nǐ lái le 'good thing you came'. 還 is hái here, not huán.

example.english: Good thing you brought an umbrella.

note: 第 + number makes ordinals: 第二 dì èr 'second'. 一 keeps its first tone here.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ dìyī cì lái Táiwān.
example.english: This is my first time in Taiwan.

note: 找 alone means 'to look for'; 到 adds success. 找不到 means 'can't find'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zhǎodào wǒ de shǒujī le.

note: For aged people and long-standing things (老朋友); old objects are 舊 jiù. Also a familiar prefix (老王, 老公) and, in speech, 'always': 他老是遲到 'he's always late'.
Counts people politely: 這位先生 'this gentleman', 幾位？ 'how many in your party?'. Also 'seat, place' in 位子 wèi zi.
Measure word for kinds of things: 這種 'this kind', 哪種 'which kind'. Other reading zhòng means 'to plant' (種花 'plant flowers').

example.pinyin: Wǒ bù xǐhuān zhè zhǒng tiānqì.
example.english: I don't like this kind of weather.

note: After another verb it shows direction away from the speaker and is said lightly as guò qu: 走過去 'walk over'. Compare 過來 'come over'.

example.trad: 你先過去，我等一下就來。
example.simp: 你先过去，我等一下就来。
example.pinyin: Nǐ xiān guòqù, wǒ děng yīxià jiù lái.
example.english: You go over first, I'll be there in a bit.

hint: one syllable; after a verb: turn X into Y
note: Usually follows another verb: 變成 'turn into', 換成 'change to', 切成 'cut into'. Alone, 成了 means 'became'.

example.pinyin: Bāng wǒ bǎ píngguǒ qiēchéng liǎng bàn.
example.english: Cut the apple in half for me.

note: MOE marks the second syllable neutral; many Taiwanese say huí lái. After a verb it means 'back here': 拿回來 'bring back'. Compare 回去 'go back'.

example.english: What time are you coming back?

note: Counts a person's age: 你幾歲？ 'how old are you?' (to a child or peer). For elders, ask 您多大年紀？

example.english: My daughter is five this year.

note: An indefinite plural measure word: 這些 'these', 那些 'those', 一些 'some', 有些 'some (of them)'. A literary particle reading suò exists but is very rare.
Taiwan (MOE) says guān xì with a full fourth tone; mainland usually guān xi. 沒關係 'it's OK, never mind' is extremely common.
Marks who does or decides something: 由你決定 'it's up to you'. Somewhat formal; casual 'from' is usually 從.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì yóu nǐ juédìng.
example.english: It's up to you to decide.

hint: before a point in time; earlier
note: Goes after the event: 吃飯之前 'before eating'. Alone it means 'previously'. Close to 以前, which leans more toward 'in the old days'.
Goes before the verb: 你先走 'you go first'. Pattern 先…再… 'first…then…'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ xiān chī, bùyòng děng wǒ.
example.english: Go ahead and eat, don't wait for me.

note: Also means going somewhere for fun: 去台灣玩. Taiwan says 玩, not mainland 玩兒; instruments use 彈 and ball sports 打. Other reading wàn appears in literary words like 古玩 'antiques'.

example.english: Where should we go for fun this weekend?

hint: after an event; not 'in the future'
note: Goes after the event: 下班之後 'after work'. Close to 以後, which also means 'in the future'.

example.pinyin: Xiàbān zhīhòu nǐ yào zuò shénme?
example.english: What are you doing after work?

note: Common set phrases: 不好意思 'excuse me / sorry', 有意思 'interesting'. MOE gives a light second syllable; many Taiwanese say yì sī with a full first tone.

gloss: to eat; to have a meal
note: Means eating a meal in general, not only rice. 吃飽了沒？ chī bǎo le méi 'have you eaten?' is a friendly Taiwan greeting. It splits around other words: 吃完飯 'after eating'.

gloss: to know; to get to know
note: To know or get acquainted with a person (or recognize a word or place). For knowing a fact, use 知道. Many Taiwanese say rèn shì with a full tone.

gloss: to carry out; to be underway
note: Somewhat formal; used for ongoing processes: 會議正在進行 'the meeting is underway'.
In Taiwan, 女生 is the everyday, polite word for women of any age; 女人 can sound blunt or emphasize womanhood.

example.pinyin: Tā shì ge hěn lìhài de nǚrén.

note: Used in statements and suggestions; in an either-or question use 還是 instead (你要茶還是咖啡？). 或 is a shorter, more formal form.

example.trad: 你明天或者後天來都可以。
example.simp: 你明天或者后天来都可以。
example.pinyin: Nǐ míngtiān huòzhě hòutiān lái dōu kěyǐ.
example.english: You can come tomorrow or the day after.

gloss: to do; to be up to; to mess up
hint: slangy, as in "what are you up to?!"
note: Casual all-purpose verb: 搞錯 gǎo cuò (get it wrong), 搞清楚 (figure out), 搞什麼 (what are you doing?!). Very common in Taiwan in set phrases (搞定 'sorted', 搞不好 'maybe'); 弄 is the gentler 'fiddle with / make'.

example.english: What on earth are you doing?

note: For gaining something abstract or earned (a chance, an answer, help). For physically picking something up, 拿到 is more natural.

example.trad: 他終於得到這個機會了。
example.simp: 他终于得到这个机会了。
example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú dédào zhège jīhuì le.

gloss: to put; to place; to let go
note: Also 'to release / let go' (放手) and 'to have time off' (放假 fàng jià). MOE also lists a literary reading fǎng, not used in speech.
Introduces a topic and goes before a noun phrase: 關於這件事… 'about this matter…'.

example.trad: 我想問你關於工作的事。
example.simp: 我想问你关于工作的事。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng wèn nǐ guānyú gōngzuò de shì.
example.english: I want to ask you about work.

note: Also a noun, 'station / stop': 車站 (station), 下一站 (next stop).
Very common in mainland speech; Taiwanese more often say 一定 or 絕對, but 肯定 is understood. As a verb it means 'to affirm / recognize' (肯定他的努力).

hint: small numbers, needs a measure word
note: Asks about small numbers and needs a measure word: 幾個？ 幾點？ In statements it means 'a few': 幾天 (a few days). The jī reading is used in 幾乎 jī hū (almost).

example.pinyin: Nǐmen jiā yǒu jǐ ge rén?
example.english: How many people are in your family?

note: Goes before a number to make an ordinal: 第一 (first), 第二次 (the second time), 第三個 (the third one).

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ dì'èr cì lái Táiwān.
example.english: This is my second time in Taiwan.

note: Used for a belief that turned out false: 我以為你走了 'I thought you'd left (but you hadn't)'. For a real opinion use 覺得 or 認為.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǐwéi nǐ jīntiān bù lái.
example.english: I thought you weren't coming today.

note: More formal than 裡 / 裡面; common in set phrases: 室內 (indoors), 國內 (domestic), 三天內 (within three days). MOE also lists an archaic reading nà.

example.pinyin: Zhège yào zài sān tiān nèi zuòwán.
example.english: This has to be finished within three days.

example.trad: 晚上一個人走路不安全。
example.simp: 晚上一个人走路不安全。
example.pinyin: Wǎnshang yī ge rén zǒulù bù ānquán.
example.english: It's not safe to walk alone at night.

note: Counts tops and coats (一件衣服, 一件外套), matters and events (一件事), and pieces of luggage. Pants and skirts use 條 instead.
Literally 'there is a person'. In questions it means 'anyone': 有人在家嗎？ 'Is anyone home?'

example.english: Someone was looking for you just now.

hint: giving up on something; let it go
note: Said when dropping a plan or an argument: 算了，不用了 suàn le, bù yòng le 'forget it, no need'. 算 suàn alone means 'to calculate; to count as'.

example.pinyin: Tā dào xiànzài hái méi chūxiàn.

note: Used for people's height (他很高), buildings, prices and levels (價錢很高).
Counts books, notebooks and magazines: 一本書. As a prefix it means 'this / one's own / original': 本來 (originally), 本人 (oneself).

example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū nǐ kànwán le ma?

note: For durations: 一個小時 (one hour). Clock time uses 點 (三點 'three o'clock'). Taiwanese also say 鐘頭 zhōng tóu.

example.pinyin: Wǒ děng le nǐ yī ge xiǎoshí.
example.english: I waited for you for an hour.

note: Short for 總是 'always' (他總遲到), and also 'sooner or later / after all' (總會好的 'it'll get better eventually'). As a prefix it means 'total / chief': 總共, 總統.
A real compliment, closer to 'pretty good' than a grudging 'not bad'. In writing it can also mean 'correct' (不錯，就是他); in speech say 對.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn de cài hěn bùcuò.
example.english: The food at this place is pretty good.

gloss: to give (as a gift); to deliver
note: Also 'to deliver' (送貨) and 'to take someone somewhere / see off': 我送你回家 'I'll take you home'.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ sòng nǐ de lǐwù.
example.english: This is a present for you.

note: A blend of 了 + 啊, very common in Taiwan to soften or push a point: 好啦 'okay, okay', 不要啦 'no, don't'. The first-tone lā appears in 啦啦隊 lā lā duì (cheerleaders) and in sound effects.

example.english: If we get the chance, let's eat together again.

note: In casual speech 手 can mean the whole arm. As a suffix it marks a skilled person: 歌手 (singer), 高手 (expert).

example.pinyin: Chīfàn qián yào xiān xǐ shǒu.
example.english: Wash your hands before you eat.

note: Describes a manner or kind: 不要那樣做 'don't do it like that'; opposite of 這樣. MOE also lists nǎ yàng, an old spelling of 哪樣 'which way'.

gloss: (place in a ranking; counter for people)
note: 'Place / rank': 第一名 (first place). Also a formal measure word for people (三名學生); in conversation use 個 or the polite 位. As a noun it means 'name' or 'fame' (有名 'famous').

example.pinyin: Tā zhècì kǎo le dìyī míng.
example.english: He came first in the exam this time.

note: Also written 了解. Means understanding someone or something thoroughly, or finding out about it: 我去瞭解一下 'I'll look into it'. Compare 明白 / 懂 (get it).

example.english: You don't understand me at all.

note: Fairly formal; in conversation Taiwanese usually just say 人 or 大家 (現在的人都很忙 'people these days are busy').

example.trad: 人們常說，時間就是金錢。
example.simp: 人们常说，时间就是金钱。
example.pinyin: Rénmen cháng shuō, shíjiān jiù shì jīnqián.
example.english: People often say time is money.

note: 看電影 'to see a movie'; a movie theater is 電影院.

example.pinyin: Zhōumò yào bù yào qù kàn diànyǐng?
example.english: Want to go see a movie this weekend?

note: Counts long, thin or flexible things: roads (路), rivers, fish (魚), pants (褲子), towels, and items of news or rules (一條新聞). For dogs Taiwan uses 隻.

hint: get approved, not pass by a place
note: Mainly 'to pass' a test, inspection or vote (考試通過了). For 'through / by means of', Taiwan says 透過 tòu guò (透過朋友認識的); 'by means of' 通過 sounds mainland.

hint: one syllable; before a measure or time word
note: Needs a measure word or time word after it: 每個人, 每天, 每次. Usually paired with 都: 每天都… 'every day…'.
In Taiwan 男生 is the everyday word for a guy of almost any age; 男人 sounds more grown-up or emphatic. MOE's neutral-tone nán ren is a different, colloquial sense, 'husband'; for 'man' it is nán rén.
Spoken ní hǎo (3rd-tone change). Common with strangers and in shops; friends usually just say 嗨 hāi or start talking.

example.pinyin: Nǐ hǎo, wǒ yào yī bēi kāfēi.
example.english: Hi, I'd like a cup of coffee.

hint: one syllable; before yī + measure word
note: Usually followed by 一 + measure word: 另一個 'the other one', 另一種 'another kind'. 另外 is the standalone form ('besides').

example.pinyin: Wǒmen huàn lìng yī jiā ba.

note: MOE: míng zi for 'name' (its míng zì is the classical 'given name + courtesy name'). Many Taiwanese say a full-tone míng zì in casual speech.

hint: how things turned out, often unexpectedly
note: Mostly used at the start of a clause when telling a story, meaning 'and then it turned out…': 結果他沒來 'in the end he didn't come'. Also the noun 'result' (考試結果).

example.trad: 我等了很久，結果他沒來。
example.simp: 我等了很久，结果他没来。
example.pinyin: Wǒ děng le hěn jiǔ, jiéguǒ tā méi lái.
example.english: I waited ages, and in the end he didn't come.

note: For any quantity, especially prices: 多少錢？ 'How much?'. Unlike 幾 it needs no measure word. Mainland speech often says duō shao; Taiwan keeps the third tone.
Marks something as obvious, or coaxes and pleads: 本來就是嘛 'that's just how it is', 快點嘛 'come on, hurry up'. The má reading appears in 幹嘛 gàn má 'what for?'.

example.english: Come on, don't be like that!
I walk to school every day.

gloss: to take part in; to attend
note: For events and activities (a party, a wedding, a contest). Joining a group or team is usually 加入.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xià ge yuè yào cānjiā bǐsài.
example.english: I'm entering a competition next month.

note: Formal or written; in conversation say 爸爸 or 爸. Mainland speech often says fù qin.
'Only have / there is only': 我只有一個. With 才 it means 'only if / only … can': 只有你才能幫我 'only you can help me'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ shēnshàng zhǐyǒu yī bǎi kuài.
example.english: I only have a hundred dollars on me.

note: On its own means 'in the past / used to': 我以前住這裡. After a time or event it means 'before': 吃飯以前. 之前 is similar but points to a specific moment.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǐqián hěn xǐhuān dǎ qiú.
example.english: I used to love playing ball.

note: 真的嗎？ 'Really?'; 真的假的？ is the classic Taiwan 'Seriously?!'. Also an adjective 'real, true': 這是真的.
A sports match or contest, not a game you play for fun (that's 遊戲). Also a verb: 我們來比賽 'let's race / compete'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ zuótiān yǒu kàn bǐsài ma?
example.english: Did you watch the game yesterday?

hint: two syllables, most common spoken 'but'; not dàn shì
note: The everyday spoken 'but', a little softer than 但是; 不過 is milder still. Also emphatic 'really': 這可是我的 'this is mine, you know'.

example.trad: 我很想去，可是我沒時間。
example.simp: 我很想去，可是我没时间。
example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xiǎng qù, kěshì wǒ méi shíjiān.
example.english: I'd love to go, but I don't have time.

note: Formal or written; in conversation Taiwanese say 沒辦法 or 不能.
More formal than 幫 / 幫忙 and also works as a noun: 謝謝你的幫助 'thanks for your help'. 很有幫助 'very helpful' is the most common everyday use. Casually you'd say 幫我一下.

example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū duì wǒ hěn yǒu bāngzhù.

note: Mostly used with a negative for emphasis: 我根本不知道 'I had no idea at all'. As an adjective it means 'fundamental' (根本的問題).
As an adverb 'especially / extra': 特別好. As an adjective 'special, unusual': 很特別.

example.english: The weather is especially nice today.

note: Used for clothes, shoes and socks. Hats, glasses and watches use 戴 dài instead.

example.pinyin: Jīntiān hěn lěng, duō chuān yīdiǎn.
example.english: It's cold today, so wear a bit more.

note: 跟…生氣 gēn … shēng qì 'be angry with…'; 不要生氣 bù yào shēng qì 'don't be mad'. 氣 qì alone means 'to make someone angry' (氣死我了 qì sǐ wǒ le 'it drives me crazy').
Taiwan (MOE) says bié rén with a full second tone; mainland speech often has neutral bié ren.

example.english: Don't worry about what other people say.

hint: two syllables, a bit formal; also 'a choice'
note: In casual speech 選 alone is common: 你選哪個？
Usually paired with 就 jiù: 只要…就… "as long as…, then…". Compare 只有…才… "only if…".

example.english: As long as you like it, that's all that matters.

note: For an event coming to an end. For finishing an action, put 完 wán after the verb (吃完 "finish eating").

example.english: What time does the movie end?

note: In Taiwan it usually means the PRC / mainland China; people also say 大陸 dà lù "the mainland".

example.pinyin: Tā míngnián yào qù Zhōngguó gōngzuò.
example.english: He's going to work in China next year.

note: Counted with 張 zhāng: 一張照片. 相片 xiàng piàn means the same.
MOE reads guò lai (neutral 來), like 回來 huí lai; many Taiwanese say a full guò lái when it is the main verb. After a verb it means toward the speaker: 拿過來 "bring it over".
Often starts a sentence: 有些人… "some people…". Before an adjective it means "a bit": 有些累 "a bit tired".

example.pinyin: Yǒuxiē rén bù xǐhuān chī là.
example.english: Some people don't like spicy food.

gloss: as (in the role of); to act as
note: Somewhat formal. 為 is wéi here, not wèi "for". 作為朋友 "as a friend".

example.pinyin: Zuòwéi péngyǒu, wǒ yīnggāi bāng nǐ.
example.english: As your friend, I should help you.

note: Big numbers are counted in 萬: 十萬 = 100,000, 一百萬 = one million. 一萬 is spoken yí wàn (tone change of 一).

example.pinyin: Zhè zhī shǒujī yào sān wàn kuài.
example.english: This phone costs thirty thousand dollars.

note: One hundred is 一百. MOE also lists a literary reading bó, not used in speech.

example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū sān bǎi kuài.
example.english: This book is three hundred dollars.

note: Two thousand is 兩千 liǎng qiān. Prices in Taiwan are often in the thousands: 三千塊.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu liǎng qiān kuài.
example.english: This shirt costs two thousand dollars.

note: X以後 = "after X"; on its own it means "later on, in the future". 之後 is very similar; for "afterwards" about past events, use 後來 hòu lái.

example.pinyin: Xiàbān yǐhòu wǒ qù zhǎo nǐ.
example.english: I'll come find you after work.

note: Colloquially also "to go (somewhere)": 你跑去哪裡了？ The rare reading páo means "to paw the ground".
Mostly a prefix (女生, 女朋友, 女兒). 女的 is a casual "a woman". Classical readings nǜ / rǔ are not used in speech.

hint: two syllables; also a defiant 'so what?'
note: Very common in Taiwan: 你覺得怎樣？ "What do you think?"; 不怎樣 "not great"; 你想怎樣？ "What do you want?" (can sound confrontational). Compare 怎麼 "how (to do)".

example.english: What do you think of this one?

note: 看醫生 = "to see a doctor". Mainland 大夫 dài fu is not used in Taiwan.

example.english: You should go see a doctor.

hint: a young girl; a bit written
note: Often 小女孩 "little girl" or 女孩子. In Taiwan, 女生 is the everyday word for a girl or young woman.

example.english: That little girl is so cute.

note: MOE gives ér zǐ with a full third tone; mainland and much casual speech say ér zi (neutral).

example.english: His son starts college this year.

note: The textbook reply to 謝謝. In everyday Taiwan speech 不會 bú huì 'no problem' is even more common, and 不客氣 can sound a little formal. 不 is spoken bú before kè. MOE gives a full tone on 氣; many speakers say a light qi.

example.trad: 不客氣，這是我應該做的。
example.simp: 不客气，这是我应该做的。
example.pinyin: Bùkèqì, zhè shì wǒ yīnggāi zuò de.
example.english: You're welcome, it was the least I could do.

hint: one syllable; become different by itself
note: Often 變 + adjective + 了: 變胖了 "got fatter". 變成 = "to turn into". To change something on purpose is 改變 or 改.

example.trad: 政府應該多蓋一點房子。
example.simp: 政府应该多盖一点房子。
example.pinyin: Zhèngfǔ yīnggāi duō gài yīdiǎn fángzi.
example.english: The government should build more housing.

note: Same idea as 那時候. Read as dàng shí, it means "right away, on the spot" (rare).

example.english: I was only ten at the time.

note: MOE lists both xià lái and xià lai. After verbs it shows going down or settling: 坐下來 "sit down", 停下來 "stop", 寫下來 "write it down".
Very common in set phrases: 算了 "forget it", 不算 "doesn't count", 還算 "fairly", 打算 "to plan".

example.pinyin: Nǐ bāng wǒ suàn yīxià duōshǎo qián.
example.english: Can you work out how much it comes to?

hint: glad; as in 'nice to meet you'
note: 興 is xìng here; its other reading xīng is in 興奮 xīng fèn "excited". 開心 is the more casual everyday word.

gloss: to bear; to suffer; to undergo
note: Mostly in compounds: 受不了 "can't stand it", 受傷 "get hurt", 接受 "to accept". 受到 is a formal "to receive"; getting mail or gifts is 收到 shōu dào.

example.english: I really can't take it anymore.

note: Counts movies, games, rains, illnesses: 一場電影, 一場雨. Taiwan (MOE) reads it cháng, also in 市場, 機場, 現場; chǎng is the mainland standard and is also common in Taiwan speech.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen qù kàn yī cháng diànyǐng ba.

note: 玩遊戲 = "to play games". Video games are also called 電動 diàn dòng in Taiwan (打電動).

example.pinyin: Tā měitiān dōu zài wán yóuxì.

gloss: to demand; to ask of; requirement
note: 要 is read yāo here, not yào.

example.pinyin: Tā duì zìjǐ yāoqiú hěn gāo.

note: Used for durations: 五分鐘 "five minutes". Clock times use 分 alone: 三點十分 "3:10".
Compare 一定 "certainly, must" and 肯定 "definitely".
As a noun suffix it is neutral tou: 石頭 "stone", 裡頭 "inside". Also counts cattle: 一頭牛.
On its own, 早！ is a casual "Morning!" (also 早安).

example.english: How come you're so early today?

note: Part of many feeling words: 小心, 開心, 放心, 擔心, 心情. The physical organ is 心臟 xīn zàng.
Introduces an extreme case, often with 連…都: 他甚至連飯都沒吃 "he didn't even eat".

example.trad: 他很忙，甚至沒時間吃飯。
example.simp: 他很忙，甚至没时间吃饭。
example.pinyin: Tā hěn máng, shènzhì méi shíjiān chīfàn.
example.english: He's so busy he doesn't even have time to eat.

note: The official spelling is 臺灣; 台灣 is the everyday form. 台 alone is short for Taiwan: 台北, 台語 (Taiwanese Hokkien).
記得 + verb = "remember to…": 記得帶傘 "remember to bring an umbrella". 得 is neutral de here (other readings dé, děi).

gloss: wait a moment; in a bit; etc.
note: Said alone it means "Wait!". In Taiwan it also means "in a bit, later": 我等等再打給你. After a list it means "etc.".
Often 談一談 / 談談 "have a talk"; 談戀愛 "to date, be in a relationship". Casual chatting is 聊 liáo.
Counted with 隻 zhī: 一隻狗. 狗狗 is a cute way to say it.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu yī zhī gǒu.
example.english: We have a dog at home.

note: 每 + measure word + noun; 個 is the default: 每個人 "everyone", 每個月 "every month". 個 is light (ge), sometimes full gè.

example.pinyin: Měige rén dōu hěn xǐhuān tā.

note: Can take an object (改變計畫 "change the plan"). Compare 變 "to become different".
Mostly after a verb: 吃完 "finish eating", 做完 "finish doing", 用完 "used up".
Everyday speech more often says 不一樣. 不同的 + noun = "different (kinds of)…".
連 X 都/也… = "even X…": 連他都知道 "even he knows". As a verb it means "to connect": 連網路 "connect to the internet".

example.pinyin: Tā lián yī jù huà dōu méi shuō.
example.english: He didn't even say a word.

note: Formal. In speech, people usually say 這樣 or 這麼, but 原來如此 "I see!" is very common.

example.english: I see, now I get it.

gloss: to see; to catch sight of
note: Means the same as 看到 kàn dào, which is more common in everyday speech. MOE gives a neutral-tone 見 (kàn jian); kàn jiàn is also commonly heard.

example.trad: 你有沒有看見我的手機？
example.simp: 你有没有看见我的手机？
example.pinyin: Nǐ yǒu méiyǒu kànjian wǒ de shǒujī?

note: Adds emphasis, often with mild annoyance: 真是的！ zhēn shì de 'honestly!'. Taiwan keeps the full tone on 是 (mainland often zhēn shi).

example.pinyin: Jīntiān zhēn shì tài rè le!
example.english: It's really way too hot today!

note: Counts flat things: paper, photos, tickets, tables, beds, faces (一張紙 yī zhāng zhǐ). Also a very common surname. The reading zhàng is rare.
Taiwan keeps the full tone on 面 (mainland often lǐ mian). Goes after a noun: 冰箱裡面 'inside the fridge'.

hint: one of a group just mentioned
note: Refers back to a group just mentioned: 其中一個 qí zhōng yī ge 'one of them'.

example.trad: 我有三個孩子，其中一個在美國。
example.simp: 我有三个孩子，其中一个在美国。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu sān ge háizi, qízhōng yī ge zài Měiguó.
example.english: I have three kids; one of them is in America.

gloss: to fall; to drop; to lose
note: After another verb it means 'away, off': 丟掉 diū diào 'throw away', 忘掉 wàng diào 'forget completely'.
Also used for taking transport: 坐捷運 zuò jié yùn 'take the MRT'. Taiwan also often says 搭 dā for this.

example.pinyin: Nǐ xiān zuò yīxià, wǒ mǎshàng lái.
example.english: Have a seat, I'll be right there.

note: Agrees to a request ('can you help me?' 'no problem!'), or says nothing is wrong: 這樣沒問題 zhè yàng méi wèn tí 'this is fine'. Built from 沒 méi + 問題 wèn tí 'problem'.

example.pinyin: Méi wèntí, jiāo gěi wǒ ba!
example.english: No problem, leave it to me!

note: A more formal version of 讓 ràng, which is far more common in speech. Also seen in 使用 shǐ yòng 'to use'. The reading shì (envoy) is literary.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì shǐ tā hěn nánguò.

note: Usually paired with 但是 dàn shì or 可是 kě shì in the next clause: 雖然很貴，但是很好吃 'it's pricey, but tasty'.

example.pinyin: Suīrán hěn lèi, dànshì hěn kāixīn.

note: A very common hedge: 好像是 'I think it's…'. Also 'to look just like' in 好像…一樣.
Combines widely: 發訊息 fā xùn xí 'send a message', 發燒 fā shāo 'have a fever', 發脾氣 fā pí qì 'lose one's temper'. 髮 fǎ (hair, as in 頭髮) is a different character.

example.pinyin: Wǒ děng yīxià fā xùnxí gěi nǐ.
example.english: I'll send you a message in a bit.

hint: a way to solve a problem
note: 沒辦法 méi bàn fǎ 'there's no way / it can't be helped' is extremely common.

example.pinyin: Méi bànfǎ, wǒmen zhǐ néng děng.
example.english: Nothing we can do; we just have to wait.

note: Polyphone: the other reading hè means 'to shout', as in 喝采 hè cǎi 'to cheer'; rare in speech.

example.english: What would you like to drink?

note: Common as 好美 hǎo měi 'so beautiful'. Also short for America (美國), as in 美金 měi jīn 'US dollars'.

example.english: The view here is so beautiful!

example.pinyin: Wǒ zhèngzài kāichē, děng yīxià dǎ gěi nǐ.
example.english: I'm driving; I'll call you back in a bit.

example.pinyin: Qíshí wǒ bù tài xǐhuān chī là.
example.english: Actually, I don't really like spicy food.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ zhēnzhèng de péngyǒu.
example.english: He's a true friend of mine.

gloss: to divide; to share; minute; point
note: Also a minute in clock time (三點十分 sān diǎn shí fēn), a point or grade, or a cent. Other reading fèn, as in 部分 bù fèn and 過分 guò fèn 'excessive'.

example.trad: 講個故事給我聽好不好？

example.pinyin: Jiǎng ge gùshi gěi wǒ tīng hǎo bù hǎo?
example.english: Will you tell me a story?

note: Taiwan says bù fèn (also written 部份); MOE's headword gives bù fen for this sense, as does mainland speech. 大部分 dà bù fèn 'most'.

example.pinyin: Dà bùfèn de rén dōu tóngyì.

note: Goes right before the verb: 我剛到 wǒ gāng dào 'I just got here'. Means the same as 剛剛 gāng gāng.

example.english: I just got off work, so tired.

note: 餓死了 'starving' is very common. The opposite is 飽 bǎo 'full'.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì wǒ lái chǔlǐ.

example.pinyin: Nǐ dàodǐ yào bù yào qù?
example.english: So are you going or not?

gloss: to contact; to get in touch
note: The usual Taiwan word; the mainland more often says 聯繫 lián xì.

example.pinyin: Dào le zài gēn nǐ liánluò.
example.english: I'll get in touch when I arrive.

note: More formal than 進 jìn or 進去 jìn qù; used for entering a place, a company, a stage.

example.pinyin: Tā jìnrù le yī jiā xīn gōngsī.

Same meaning as 能 néng, a little more formal or emphatic.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xīwàng nénggòu bāng shàng máng.

note: Counts rooms and buildings: 一間房間, 這間店. Also means 'between' (之間). Other reading jiàn, as in 間接 jiàn jiē 'indirect'.

gloss: to beg; to plead; to seek
note: Also in 求婚 qiú hūn 'to propose marriage' and 要求 yāo qiú 'to demand'.

example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān biǎoxiàn de hěn hǎo.

出門 chū mén 'to go out'. Also a measure word for school subjects: 一門課 yī mén kè.

hint: news one hears, not TV news
note: Taiwan reads 息 as xí (mainland xiāo xi). 好消息 hǎo xiāo xí 'good news'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yī ge hǎo xiāoxí!

example.english: My daughter starts elementary school this year.

note: The casual, affectionate word, also used to address him. 丈夫 is formal and 先生 is polite. With a light second syllable (lǎo gong) it is an old word for a eunuch.

example.english: My husband is a great cook.

hint: manner or style (e.g. way of paying)
note: 生活方式 shēng huó fāng shì 'lifestyle'. Compare 方法 fāng fǎ 'method' and 辦法 bàn fǎ 'solution'.

example.trad: 每個人的生活方式不一樣。
example.simp: 每个人的生活方式不一样。
example.pinyin: Měi ge rén de shēnghuó fāngshì bù yīyàng.

gloss: to pay attention; to watch out

example.english: Watch out for cars when crossing the street.

note: A real apology. For small things (bumping someone, asking a favor) Taiwanese usually say 不好意思 bù hǎo yì si.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yuànyì jià gěi wǒ ma?

example.trad: 我今天一定要完成這個報告。
example.simp: 我今天一定要完成这个报告。
example.pinyin: Wǒ jīntiān yīdìng yào wánchéng zhège bàogào.
example.english: I have to finish this report today.

note: As praise: 好棒！ hǎo bàng 'awesome!' Literally 'stick, club', as in 棒球 bàng qiú 'baseball'.

example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zhèngzài diàochá zhè jiàn shì.

hint: taking action, not a body movement
note: 行 here is xíng; it is háng in 銀行 yín háng (bank). In Taiwan 行動 also means mobile: 行動電源 xíng dòng diàn yuán (power bank).

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng hē yī bēi shuǐ.
example.english: I'd like a glass of water.

note: MOE gives a neutral-tone 個 (zhěng ge); zhěng gè is also commonly heard. Also used as an adverb: 我整個傻眼 (I was totally stunned).

example.pinyin: Wǒ zhěngge xiàwǔ dōu zài shuìjiào.

note: MOE gives wǎn shang; many Taiwanese speakers say wǎn shàng with a full tone.

example.pinyin: Wǎnshang yào bù yào yīqǐ chīfàn?
example.english: Want to have dinner together tonight?

note: As a verb it means to spend: 花錢 huā qián (spend money), 花時間 huā shí jiān (spend time). Counted with 朵 duǒ.

gloss: to say; to speak; to tell
note: Very common in Taiwan speech, often used where the mainland says 說: 講中文 (speak Chinese), 講電話 (talk on the phone).

example.pinyin: Nǐ jiǎng màn yīdiǎn hǎo bù hǎo?
example.english: Could you speak a little slower?

note: Common in 排隊 pái duì (to wait in line) and 球隊 qiú duì (sports team).

example.trad: 總統今天在電視上講話。
example.simp: 总统今天在电视上讲话。
example.pinyin: Zǒngtǒng jīntiān zài diànshì shàng jiǎnghuà.
example.english: The president spoke on TV today.

note: 上大學 / 念大學 = to go to college. MOE also lists tài xué, meaning the ancient imperial academy (太學); not used in speech.
生日快樂 shēng rì kuài lè 'happy birthday'. 過生日 guò shēng rì 'to celebrate a birthday'.

example.pinyin: Jīntiān shì wǒ lǎopo de shēngrì.

note: Also 拉肚子 lā dù zi (to have diarrhea). Door signs in Taiwan say 推 (push) and 拉 (pull).

example.pinyin: Zhège mén yào yòng lā de.
example.english: You have to pull this door.

note: Introduces the topic you have an attitude or opinion about, often at the start of a sentence. A bit formal; close to 關於 guān yú (about).

example.trad: 對於這件事，我沒有意見。
example.simp: 对于这件事，我没有意见。
example.pinyin: Duìyú zhè jiàn shì, wǒ méiyǒu yìjiàn.
example.english: I have no opinion on this matter.

note: More formal than 用 yòng; common on signs and instructions.

example.english: You can't use your phone here.

note: Also a verb: 我會努力 (I'll do my best). 加油 is the cheer for it.

hint: everyday compliment; also 'nicely done', not měi
note: MOE gives a neutral-tone 亮 (piào liang); in Taiwan you will often hear piào liàng. Also means well done: 做得漂亮 (nicely done).

example.english: I want to learn to drive.

note: Shops greet you with 歡迎光臨 huān yíng guāng lín (welcome in).

example.english: You're welcome to come over to my place!

note: Used before a noun with 的: 唯一的辦法 (the only way). Different from 只 zhǐ (only, as an adverb).

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒ wéiyī de péngyǒu.

gloss: to grab; to catch; to scratch
note: 抓到 = caught; 抓癢 zhuā yǎng = scratch an itch. MOE also lists a literary reading zhāo, which is not used in speech.

hint: assure it will happen, not just agree

example.pinyin: Wǒ bǎozhèng bù huì zài chídào.
example.english: I promise I won't be late again.

note: Verb + object (說 + 話), so it takes no object: say 跟他說話 (talk to him), not 說話他.

example.pinyin: Nǐ bù yào dòng, wǒ bāng nǐ pāizhào.
example.english: Don't move, I'll take your picture.

gloss: to manage; to mind; to care about
note: 別管我 (leave me alone); 不管 bù guǎn (no matter). As a noun it means tube or pipe: 水管 shuǐ guǎn.

example.pinyin: Wǒ de shì bù yòng nǐ guǎn.
example.english: My business is none of your concern.

note: Also links clauses: 同時 (meanwhile; also). Different from 一起 (together, in company).

example.pinyin: Tāmen liǎng ge tóngshí xiào le.
example.english: They both laughed at the same time.

note: Also an adjective: 確實的消息 (reliable news).
Counted with 把 bǎ: 一把槍. MOE also lists a rare reading chēng (an old star name).

example.pinyin: Tā shǒu shàng názhe yī bǎ qiāng.
example.english: He's holding a gun in his hand.

Mostly for seeing people; for seeing things 看到 kàn dào is more usual.

example.pinyin: Bùguǎn zěnyàng, wǒ dōu zhīchí nǐ.
example.english: No matter what, I support you.

note: Movement out and away from the speaker; 出來 chū lái is out toward the speaker. Also follows verbs: 走出去 (walk out).

example.english: What time are you coming home?

hint: the same (one), as in same day
note: Mostly in set forms: 同一個 (the same one), 不同 (different), 同學 (classmate). Other reading tòng, only in 胡同 (alley).

example.pinyin: Wǒmen shì tóng yī tiān shēngrì.

example.english: I've been watching my diet lately.

gloss: to do; to make; to mess with
note: A catch-all verb: 弄壞 (to break), 弄好 (to get it done), 弄丟 (to lose). MOE's other reading is lòng (lane), as in 巷弄 and addresses, but most Taiwanese say nòng when reading an address.

example.pinyin: Nǐ bǎ wǒ de shǒujī nònghuài le!

note: Formal or written; in everyday speech people say 媽媽 mā ma. 母親節 = Mother's Day.
夠了！ (That's enough!) 不夠 (not enough). Before an adjective it can mean really: 夠辣 (plenty spicy).

example.pinyin: Wǒmen de qián gòu bù gòu?

gloss: to pick up (a person); to answer
hint: meet a person; take a call
note: 接電話 (answer the phone), 接人 (pick someone up), 接球 (catch a ball).

example.english: I'll pick you up after work.

note: Taiwan (MOE) says rèn wù with a full tone; mainland often rèn wu.

example.pinyin: Lǎobǎn gěi wǒ yī ge xīn rènwù.
example.english: The boss gave me a new task.

gloss: to take (a photo); to pat; to clap
note: 拍照 (take photos), 拍手 (clap), 拍電影 (shoot a film). MOE lists rare other readings (pā, bó, pò) not used in speech.

example.trad: 可以幫我們拍一張照嗎？
example.simp: 可以帮我们拍一张照吗？
example.pinyin: Kěyǐ bāng wǒmen pāi yī zhāng zhào ma?
example.english: Could you take a picture of us?

example.english: Thank you so much for your help.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn yǒu mài kāfēi ma?

gloss: related to; to have to do with
note: Pattern: A 跟 B 有關 (A has to do with B). In casual speech 有關係 is common.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì gēn tā yǒuguān.
example.english: This has something to do with him.

note: 不舒服 means 'feeling unwell'. MOE gives a light second syllable; many Taiwanese say shū fú.

example.english: The two of them are brothers.

example.pinyin: Tiānqì huì yǐngxiǎng wǒ de xīnqíng.

note: Taiwan (MOE) says yán jiù; mainland says yán jiū.

example.english: He does research at a university.

example.simp: 这家饭店有提供早餐吗？
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā fàndiàn yǒu tígōng zǎocān ma?

gloss: to point at; to mean; finger
note: 你是指… nǐ shì zhǐ… means "do you mean…?". As a noun it means finger, usually 手指 shǒu zhǐ.
Free of charge is 免費 miǎn fèi, not 自由.
Short form of 今天晚上 jīn tiān wǎn shang, which is just as common in speech.

example.pinyin: Jīnwǎn yào bù yào yīqǐ chīfàn?

note: Everyday short form of 選擇 xuǎn zé. Also "to elect": 選總統 elect a president. 挑 tiāo is similar but means picking out carefully.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yào xuǎn nǎ yī ge?

note: Slightly more formal than 也許 yě xǔ and 可能 kě néng, which are more common in conversation.

note: More formal than 覺得 jué de; usually followed by a feeling, e.g. 感到很高興.

example.pinyin: Nǐ kàndào jīntiān de xīnwén le ma?
