example.simp: 根据气象预报，明天会下雨。
example.pinyin: Gēnjù qìxiàng yùbào, míngtiān huì xiàyǔ.
example.english: According to the weather forecast, it'll rain tomorrow.

note: Marks a past experience, often with 過: 我曾經去過. A little formal; in speech 過 alone is common. 曾 is read zēng in 曾祖父 'great-grandfather'.
離…很遠 'far from…'. The rare literary reading yuàn means 'to keep away from'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ jiā lí zhèlǐ yuǎn bù yuǎn?
example.english: Is your place far from here?

gloss: to go down; to keep going
note: After a verb it shows going down (跳下去 'jump down') or continuing (說下去 'keep talking'). MOE marks qu as neutral; Taiwanese often say full-tone xià qù, especially for 'go down'.

example.english: It can't go on like this.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jīnnián de mùbiāo shì cún qián.
example.english: My goal this year is to save money.

note: A more formal 所以 'so'; common in news and writing.

example.trad: 他生病了，因此沒來上班。
example.simp: 他生病了，因此没来上班。
example.pinyin: Tā shēngbìng le, yīncǐ méi lái shàngbān.
example.english: He was sick, so he didn't come to work.
Hang on, I'll be right there!

note: 約朋友 'make plans with a friend', 約好了 'it's arranged', 約會 'date'. In formal speech also 'approximately': 約十分鐘. CEDICT also lists a rare reading yāo 'to weigh', not used in Taiwan.

example.english: Let's make plans to eat together tomorrow.

note: 救命！ jiù mìng 'Help!' (literally 'save life').

example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiù le tā de mìng.

note: More formal than 對不起; common in shops, at work and in messages: 很抱歉讓你久等了 'sorry to keep you waiting'.
Also 'prone to': 他很容易生病 'he gets sick easily'.
Used for weather, food and people (cold, distant). Catching a cold is 感冒 gǎn mào.

example.pinyin: Wàimiàn hǎo lěng, duō chuān yīdiǎn.
example.english: It's really cold out, wear more layers.

note: 睡覺 is the full 'to sleep / go to bed'. 睡 alone combines with other words: 睡得好 'sleep well', 睡著 shuì zháo 'fall asleep', 睡午覺 'take a nap'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ zuówǎn shuì de hǎo ma?
example.english: Did you sleep well last night?

example.pinyin: Wǒmen míngnián yào qù Rìběn wán.
example.english: We're going on a trip to Japan next year.
My older brother is a lawyer.

gloss: to be in charge of; responsible
note: 負責 + task: 他負責這個案子 'he's in charge of this project'. The noun 'responsibility' is 責任.

hint: one syllable; grasp what's said or read
note: 聽得懂 'understand (what you hear)', 看不懂 'can't understand (what you see or read)'. 我不懂 'I don't get it'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ dǒng wǒ de yìsi ma?
example.english: Do you get what I mean?

note: Opposite of 多. Polyphone: shào means 'young', as in 少年 shào nián 'youth'.
Opposite of 開: 關門 'close the door', 關燈 'turn off the light'. Also 'to lock up'.

example.english: Remember to turn off the lights when you go out.

note: Cooked rice, or a meal in general: 午飯 'lunch', 晚飯 'dinner'. Breakfast is 早餐 zǎo cān in Taiwan. Uncooked rice is 米 mǐ.

example.english: I'd like a bowl of white rice.

note: Almost always with 不/沒: 我從來沒去過 'I've never been', 他從來不喝酒 'he never drinks'. The affirmative 'always, all along' sense exists but is bookish.

example.pinyin: Gǒu shì rénlèi zuì hǎo de péngyǒu.

note: A time word, a bit more formal than 現在 'now'.
Everyday Taiwan speech uses 老婆 or 太太. The literary reading qī zǐ means 'wife and children'.
Taiwan usually writes the noun as 紀錄, which sounds the same: 破紀錄 'break a record'.

example.trad: 我每天記錄自己吃了什麼。
example.simp: 我每天记录自己吃了什么。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān jìlù zìjǐ chī le shénme.
example.english: Every day I record what I ate.

note: Goes before adjectives, usually for unwelcome things: 有點累 'a bit tired'. Taiwanese often say 有一點. Compare 一點 after the adjective: 好一點 'a bit better'.
Said when stuck: 怎麼辦？ 'What do I do?'. 該怎麼辦 'what should we do'.

example.english: My wallet's gone, what do I do?

note: 加糖 'add sugar', 加油 'go for it!', and in math 二加三 'two plus three'.

example.english: Do you want sugar in it?

note: 天氣很好 tiān qì hěn hǎo 'the weather is nice'. 天氣預報 tiān qì yù bào 'weather forecast'. Hot, muggy weather is 悶熱 mēn rè.

example.english: The weather is so hot today!

note: More formal than 得到 'to get'; used for prizes, results and support.
倒水 'pour water', 倒垃圾 'take out the trash'. dào is also an adverb 'actually, on the contrary'. Polyphone: dǎo means 'to fall over' (跌倒 dié dǎo, Taiwan reading).
Most often before adjectives or 喜歡: 這個比較便宜 'this one is cheaper'. Taiwan says jiào; mainland speech often has bǐ jiǎo.
A reply to thanks or worry, or 'nothing much': 沒什麼特別的 'nothing special'. After an apology people say 沒關係 'it's okay'.
Introduces something you heard from others: 聽說他要搬家 'I heard he's moving'.
壞了 'broken', 壞人 'bad guy'. After a verb or adjective it can mean 'terribly': 累壞了 'exhausted', 嚇壞了 'scared to death'. (MOE also lists a classical reading guài 'to destroy', not used in speech.)
In Taiwan it's the normal polite way to address a young woman or a server, and has no bad connotation. Taiwan says jiě with full tone; mainland often xiǎo jie.

example.english: Excuse me, miss, where's the restroom?

note: Counted with 件: 一件衣服 'a piece of clothing'. MOE marks fu as neutral; full-tone yī fú is also heard in Taiwan.
Counts movies and TV series: 一部電影 'a movie', 一部連續劇 'a TV series'. Also heard for cars and phones, but Taiwan more often says 一台車, 一支手機. Also 'part' or 'ministry' in 部分, 外交部.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān kàn le yī bù diànyǐng.

note: Means a dish or vegetables (青菜). Counted with 道 or 盤. Taiwan slang: 很菜 means 'a total beginner', and 菜 can mean 'my type'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī méi diàn le.
example.english: My phone is out of battery.

note: The person you call comes with 給: 打電話給媽媽 'call Mom'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ wǎn yīdiǎn dǎ diànhuà gěi nǐ.
example.english: I'll call you a bit later.

note: 聽 is 'to listen'; 聽到 means actually hearing something. 聽得到 'can hear', 聽不到 'can't hear'.
換衣服 'change clothes', 換錢 'exchange money', 換你了 'your turn'.

example.pinyin: Děng wǒ yīxià, wǒ qù huàn yīfu.
example.english: Wait for me, I'm going to change.

note: Also a verb, "to be busy with": 你在忙什麼？ (nǐ zài máng shénme?) "What are you busy with?"

example.english: What have you been busy with lately?

gloss: to keep; to save (for someone); to stay
hint: one syllable; save for later, or stay on
note: Not "to leave" as in going away (that is 離開 lí kāi). Common: 留給你 "save it for you", 留下來 "stay behind" (see 留下).

example.pinyin: Bāng wǒ liú yī ge wèizi.

hint: do something with care, before a verb
note: Used before a verb: 好好休息 "get a good rest", 好好想一想 "think it over carefully". Taiwan says hǎo hǎo, without the mainland erhua hǎo hāor.

example.english: You need to get a good rest.

note: Taiwan says 美金 in speech; 美元 (měi yuán) is the written or mainland term.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yào qù yínháng huàn měijīn.
example.english: I'm going to the bank to change money into US dollars.

note: MOE (Taiwan standard) reads 場 here as cháng; the mainland says xiàn chǎng, and many Taiwanese say chǎng too. 現場 also means "live" (a live show).

example.english: The police are already at the scene.

note: Goes before a verb: 不敢去 "don't dare to go". 我不敢相信 means "I can't believe it".

example.trad: 我晚上不敢一個人出去。
example.simp: 我晚上不敢一个人出去。
example.pinyin: Wǒ wǎnshang bù gǎn yī ge rén chūqù.
example.english: I don't dare go out alone at night.

example.trad: 我們跟他們合作很久了。
example.simp: 我们跟他们合作很久了。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen gēn tāmen hézuò hěn jiǔ le.
example.english: We've worked with them for a long time.

note: The everyday word. 洗手間 xǐ shǒu jiān is a politer word, common on signs.

example.english: I'm going to the restroom first.

gloss: to do (about it); to hold (an event)
hint: as in 'what do we do?', or throw a party
note: Very common in 怎麼辦 (zěnme bàn) "what do we do?", 辦事 "run errands", and 辦派對 "throw a party".
More about empathy and comprehension than 懂 (dǒng). 我可以理解 "I can understand (why)".

example.pinyin: Wǒ kěyǐ lǐjiě nǐ de gǎnjué.
example.english: I can understand how you feel.

note: Only for time; physical length is 長 (cháng). 多久 "how long", 好久不見 "long time no see".

example.pinyin: Hǎo jiǔ bù jiàn, nǐ zuìjìn hǎo ma?
example.english: Long time no see, how have you been?

hint: machines; Taiwan's everyday word for cars too
note: Counts machines, appliances and vehicles: 一台電腦, 一台車. As a noun it means stage or platform, and it is short for Taiwan (台灣). Formally written 臺.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng mǎi yī tái xīn diànnǎo.
example.english: I want to buy a new computer.

hint: keep up a state or condition

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn de fúwù hěn hǎo.
example.english: The service at this shop is great.

note: Also in 跳舞 (tiào wǔ) "to dance".

example.pinyin: Tā tiào de hǎo gāo o!

note: Starts a rhetorical question showing surprise or disbelief, usually ending in 嗎: 難道你不知道嗎？ "Don't tell me you didn't know?"
事實上 (shì shí shàng) means "in fact; actually".

example.pinyin: Wǒ shuō de dōu shì shìshí.

note: The second syllable is light. Often written 姊姊 in Taiwan, with the same pronunciation. Also a friendly way to address a young woman.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiějie bǐ wǒ dà sān suì.
example.english: My sister is three years older than me.

note: Both characters are polyphones: 行 is xíng here (háng in 銀行), and 為 is wéi here (wèi means "for").
Taiwan keeps the full tone, dǎ suàn; the mainland often says dǎ suan. Also a noun, "plan".

example.english: What are you planning to do this weekend?

note: Taiwan standard (MOE) is wéi xiǎn; the mainland says wēi xiǎn.

example.pinyin: Zhèlǐ hěn wéixiǎn, bù yào guòqù!
example.english: It's dangerous here, don't go over there!

note: Formal; heard mostly in set phrases like 女士優先 and 各位女士先生 "ladies and gentlemen". To address a woman Taiwanese say 小姐; in casual talk a woman is 女生 (nǚ shēng).

hint: raise a topic; lift by a handle
note: 提到 "to mention", 提醒 "to remind". In Taiwan 提防 "to be on guard against" is also tí fáng (the mainland says dī fang).

example.pinyin: Tā méi gēn wǒ tí guò zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: He never mentioned this to me.
I'll wait for you at the office.

note: "To marry someone" is 跟某人結婚 (gēn … jié hūn); 結婚 does not take a direct object.
Mostly in wishes: 生日快樂, 新年快樂. For everyday "I'm happy" Taiwanese usually say 開心 or 高興.

gloss: to go to work; to be at work
hint: the workday, at the office or job
note: 下班 xià bān is 'to get off work'. 上班族 shàng bān zú means 'office workers'.

example.english: Do you have to work tomorrow?

note: Polyphone: qiǎng in 勉強 (miǎn qiǎng) "reluctantly; to force", and jiàng in 倔強 (jué jiàng) "stubborn".
Polyphone: zhuàn means "to spin around" (轉圈 zhuàn quān). zhuǎn: 右轉 "turn right", 轉車 "change trains", 轉帳 "transfer money".
重 is chóng here ("again"), not zhòng "heavy". Unlike 再 (zài), it means starting over.

gloss: to look up; to check; to investigate
note: Read zhā only as a surname. 查一下 "look it up".
For distance: A 離 B 很近/很遠 "A is close to/far from B". Starting point "from" is 從 (cóng). Also in 離開 "to leave".

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā lí zhèlǐ hěn jìn.
example.english: My home is close to here.

hint: direction of movement, e.g. go forward
note: Used before a direction: 往前走 "go forward", 往左轉 "turn left". 向 (xiàng) is similar but more formal, and also used toward people.

example.pinyin: Yīzhí wǎng qián zǒu jiù dào le.
example.english: Just go straight ahead and you're there.

note: The physical dwelling; "home" in the family sense is 家 (jiā).
Covers both a shower and a bath. 洗 xǐ alone is 'to wash' (洗手 xǐ shǒu 'wash your hands').

example.english: I'm going to take a shower first.

note: Taiwan's usual word for "just now"; the mainland often says 剛才 (gāng cái). Taiwan keeps both tones: gāng gāng.

example.pinyin: Tā gānggāng dǎ diànhuà gěi nǐ.

note: Expresses relief after waiting. "Finally" meaning "lastly" in a list is 最後 (zuì hòu).
一方面…另一方面… means "on one hand… on the other hand…".

example.pinyin: Zhè fāngmiàn wǒ bù tài dǒng.
example.english: I don't know much about that area.

note: Often means health: 身體好嗎？ "How's your health?"

example.pinyin: Nǐ bàba shēntǐ hái hǎo ma?
example.english: Is your dad in good health?

note: Said to children or a partner, like "sweetie". A newborn baby is 嬰兒 (yīng ér) or 小寶寶.
Close to 怕 (pà), which is shorter and more casual and also means "to worry that…".
Also a polite title for teachers and some professionals: 王老師.

example.pinyin: Tā shì wǒmen de Yīngwén lǎoshī.

note: Taiwan colloquial, often with 的: 蠻好的 "pretty good". The mainland says 挺 (tǐng). Many Taiwanese say mǎn here (written 滿).

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn mán hǎochī de.
example.english: The food at this place is pretty good.

note: 有精神 "full of energy", 沒精神 "listless"; 精神病 is "mental illness". The mainland reads the "lively" sense jīng shen; Taiwan says jīng shén for both.

example.trad: 你今天看起來很有精神。
example.simp: 你今天看起来很有精神。
example.pinyin: Nǐ jīntiān kàn qǐlái hěn yǒu jīngshén.
example.english: You look full of energy today.

note: Polyphone: chóng means "again" or "layer" (重新 chóng xīn "anew", 重複 "to repeat").
The second syllable is light.

example.english: My younger brother is in college.

note: Often split around the object: 帶朋友來 "bring a friend".

example.pinyin: Tā dàilái le yī ge hǎo xiāoxí.

hint: the time to come, in general
note: Close to 將來 (jiāng lái); 將來 is more about one's own plans ("when I grow up"), 未來 about the future in general.

example.pinyin: Wèilái de shì, shéi zhīdào ne?
example.english: Who knows what the future holds?

note: A notable or newsworthy incident; an everyday "matter, thing" is 事情 (shì qíng).
Used in pairs: 越A越B 'the more A, the more B' (越吃越胖 yuè chī yuè pàng); 越來越 yuè lái yuè 'more and more'. On its own it can also mean 'to cross over' (越過).

example.pinyin: Yǔ yuè xià yuè dà le.
example.english: The rain is getting heavier and heavier.

note: 天黑了 tiān hēi le means 'it's gotten dark (night is falling)'. As a color word it is usually 黑色 hēi sè. MOE also lists a literary reading hè, not used in speech.

example.pinyin: Tiān hēi le, wǒmen huíjiā ba.
example.english: It's dark now, let's go home.

note: At the start of a sentence it means 'also, besides'. Before a number + measure word it means 'the other / another': 另外一杯 lìng wài yī bēi 'another cup'.

example.pinyin: Lìngwài, wǒ hái yào yī bēi chá.
example.english: Also, I'd like a cup of tea.

note: For a bad situation, illness or problem. 'Serious' meaning earnest or hard-working is 認真 rèn zhēn.
The most common everyday word for feeling happy or having fun. 高興 is 'glad, pleased'; 快樂 is used mostly in wishes like 生日快樂.

example.english: We had a lot of fun today.

note: The second syllable is light. Also used affectionately for a little girl.

example.english: My younger sister works in Taipei.

note: Mostly used in compounds: 工作人員 gōng zuò rén yuán 'staff', 服務人員 'service staff'.

example.trad: 有問題可以問工作人員。
example.simp: 有问题可以问工作人员。
example.pinyin: Yǒu wèntí kěyǐ wèn gōngzuò rényuán.
example.english: If you have a question, you can ask the staff.

note: Formal word used in news and official reports. In conversation, 'to die' is just 死 sǐ.

example.pinyin: Zhè cì chēhuò méiyǒu rén sǐwáng.
example.english: No one died in this car accident.

note: 這 'this' + 次 'time, occurrence'. Likewise 上次 'last time', 下次 'next time'. Casual speech also says zhèi cì (MOE lists zhèi as a variant of 這).
Also a noun, 'checkup / inspection'. 查 alone means 'to look up'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yào qù yīyuàn jiǎnchá yīxià.
example.english: You should go get checked at the hospital.

note: Join a group, team or club. For taking part in an event, use 參加 cān jiā. It can also mean 'to add' an ingredient.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yào bù yào jiārù wǒmen?
example.english: Do you want to join us?

note: 很一般 'pretty average, nothing special'; 一般人 'ordinary people'; 一般來說 'generally speaking'. For 'usually' Taiwanese tend to say 通常 or 平常. Spoken yì bān (一 changes tone before a 1st tone).

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn de dōngxi hěn yībān.
example.english: This shop's stuff is pretty average.

note: Polyphone: jiāo is the verb 'to teach'; jiào in compounds like 教室 jiào shì 'classroom', 教育 'education' and 宗教 'religion'.
Something stops (雨停了 'the rain stopped') or you park a vehicle: 停車 tíng chē. Telling someone 'stop it!' is usually 不要 or 別.

example.pinyin: Yǔ tíng le, wǒmen zǒu ba.
example.english: The rain has stopped, let's go.

note: Material or data you look up or hand in, such as documents or files. News or updates are 消息 xiāo xí; 資訊 is 'information' in a broader sense.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zài wǎnglù shàng zhǎo zīliào.

note: 回 'return' + 到 'arrive'; always followed by a place or state: 回到家 'get home'. Compare 回來 'come back' and 回去 'go back'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ shí diǎn cái huídào jiā.
example.english: I didn't get home until ten.

note: Very Taiwanese. Ends a sentence to show surprise or excitement: 好好吃耶 'wow, this is so good!'. Said with a high level tone (yē), sometimes lighter in fast speech; the other reading yé is a classical question particle.

example.english: Wow, this cake is so good!

note: Slightly formal; in casual talk Taiwanese often say 爸媽 bà mā 'mom and dad'.

example.english: My parents live in the south.

hint: all of it; can stand alone
note: Can stand alone ('all of it') or come before a noun with 的: 全部的人 'everyone'. Compare 所有 'all (the)' and 都 'all, both'.
…的樣子 at the end of a sentence means 'seems / looks like…': 很累的樣子 'looks tired'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ hǎoxiàng hěn lèi de yàngzi.

note: Also 'face' in the social sense: 丟臉 diū liǎn 'to lose face, embarrassing'.

example.english: I'll go wash my face first.

note: 打球 dǎ qiú 'to play ball' (basketball, baseball and similar); 踢球 tī qiú 'to play soccer'.
Usually said with 了: 我忘了 'I forgot'. Means the same as 忘記 wàng jì. The literary reading wáng is not used in speech.

example.english: I forgot to bring my keys.

note: Any line, string, cable or route (an MRT or bus line). The measure word is 條 tiáo.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo xiàn tài duǎn le.

note: Usually followed by 都 dōu: 每天都… 'every day (without fail)…'.

hint: rice and dishes in a box
note: A Taiwan staple: rice with a main dish and sides, bought for lunch or dinner (排骨便當 pái gǔ biàn dāng 'pork chop bento'). The word comes from Japanese bentō. MOE also lists biàn dang with a light second syllable. 便 is biàn here, not pián as in 便宜.

example.english: I'm having a bento for lunch.

note: Counts sets such as glasses (一副眼鏡), gloves and decks of cards, and facial expressions (一副很累的樣子 'looking all tired'). As a prefix it means 'vice- / deputy': 副總統 'vice president'. A rare literary reading is pì.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xūyào yī fù xīn yǎnjìng.
example.english: I need a new pair of glasses.

gloss: to make use of; to exploit
note: It can be neutral ('make good use of time') or negative ('use / exploit a person'). For plain 'to use' a tool, say 用.

example.english: You should make good use of your time.

note: A casual and slightly cheeky way to refer to a person: 這傢伙 'this guy'. It can sound rude about a stranger.
Both the verb and the noun: 設計師 shè jì shī 'designer'.

example.trad: 這件衣服的設計很特別。
example.simp: 这件衣服的设计很特别。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu de shèjì hěn tèbié.
example.english: This outfit has a really unusual design.

note: Insist on something (堅持要… 'insist on…') or keep going without giving up (再堅持一下 'hang in there a bit longer').

hint: with a finger, like a button
note: Press with a finger: buttons, doorbells, keys. Pushing a door or person is 推 tuī. In formal speech 按照 means 'according to'.
Polyphone: dāi 'to stay (somewhere)'; dài in 等待 'to wait', 對待 'to treat (someone)' and 待遇 'pay, treatment'. Compare 住 zhù 'to live somewhere'.

example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒ xiǎng dāi zài jiālǐ.
example.english: This weekend I want to stay home.

gloss: to be affected by; to receive
note: Means you undergo or experience something, usually followed by an abstract noun: 受到影響 'be affected', 受到歡迎 'be welcomed', 受到批評 'be criticized'. Don't confuse it with 收到 shōu dào 'to receive (a package or message)'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ bùyào zhème kuài jiù fàngqì.

note: Taiwan usually says 早餐 (the mainland often says 早飯). The 早餐店 zǎo cān diàn 'breakfast shop' is a Taiwan institution. Lunch is 午餐 wǔ cān or 午飯 wǔ fàn.
'Late' in time (太晚了 'it's too late', 晚一點 'a bit later'), and 'evening' in words like 今晚 and 晚安 'good night'. The usual word for 'evening' is 晚上.

example.pinyin: Tài wǎn le, kuài qù shuìjiào.
example.english: It's too late, go to bed.

note: 好麻煩 'what a hassle'. 麻煩你… 'could you please…' is a very common polite request. MOE gives a neutral tone, má fan, but many Taiwanese say má fán.

example.english: Could you please open the door for me?

hint: all the way until, two syllables
note: Often paired with 才 cái: 直到昨天才… 'not until yesterday did…'. Don't confuse it with 知道 zhī dào 'to know', which differs only in the first tone.

example.pinyin: Tā zhídào zuótiān cái gàosu wǒ.
example.english: He didn't tell me until yesterday.

note: Taiwan standard (MOE) reading is tú rán; the mainland says tū rán. Both are understood.
Same meaning as 很多 hěn duō, which is far more common in casual speech.

example.english: There are a lot of people in the park.

note: In everyday Taiwan speech it is often 嘴巴 zuǐ ba. 嘴很甜 'sweet-talking', 閉嘴 bì zuǐ 'shut up'. 口 kǒu is 'mouth' mainly in compounds and as 'opening, entrance'.
Hurting someone physically or emotionally; also a noun, 'harm, damage'. Getting injured yourself is 受傷 shòu shāng.

example.english: I don't want to hurt you.

note: Taiwan (MOE) reads both syllables with full tones, yǎn jīng; the mainland makes the second one neutral (yǎn jing).
Go back somewhere else, away from the speaker; 回來 means 'come back here'. MOE gives a neutral tone, but Taiwanese often say huí qù, especially when it ends the sentence.
Also 晚飯 wǎn fàn. 吃晚餐 chī wǎn cān 'to have dinner'.
The somewhat formal noun. In casual talk people say 錯 cuò: 是我的錯 'it's my fault'.

example.pinyin: Zhè fèn bàogào yǒu hěn duō cuòwù.
example.english: This report has a lot of mistakes.

note: The MOE standard form is written 祕密, but 秘密 is very common in Taiwan. The pronunciation is the same.
After a time or number it means 'and a half': 三點半 'half past three', 一個半 'one and a half'. 一半 yī bàn means 'half (of it)'.
不 'not' + 再 'again'; it often ends with 了. Spoken bú zài (不 changes to a 2nd tone before a 4th tone).

example.pinyin: Tā bù zài shì xiǎoháizi le.

note: Deeper meaning or value: 很有意義 'meaningful'. The meaning of a word or what someone means is 意思 yì si.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì duì wǒ hěn yǒu yìyì.
example.english: This means a lot to me.

note: Come in toward where the speaker is; 進去 jìn qù means 'go in'. After another verb it means 'in (toward here)': 走進來 'walk in'.

example.pinyin: Mén méi suǒ, qǐng jìnlái ba.
example.english: The door's unlocked, come on in.

note: Also a noun: one's experiences or background. For know-how or skill gained, 經驗 jīng yàn is used.

example.english: She has been through a lot.

note: 行 is read háng here (a business or trade). As 'to walk / OK' it is xíng.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yào qù yínháng lǐng qián.
example.english: I need to go to the bank to take out money.

note: Counted with 把 bǎ: 一把鑰匙 yī bǎ yào shi 'a key'. MOE reads the second syllable light (yào shi).
Means going in, away from where the speaker is; 進來 jìn lái is 'come in'. Also follows other verbs: 走進去 zǒu jìn qù 'walk in'. Often pronounced lightly as jìn qu.

In Taiwan, 讀書 dú shū and 讀大學 mean 'to study / attend school'; 念 niàn (念書, 念大學) is an equally common synonym. For reading a book silently, people usually say 看書 kàn shū. The rare reading dòu means a pause in a sentence.

example.english: He goes to university in Taipei.

note: Works for doors, boxes, bottles, and switching on devices (打開電視 dǎ kāi diàn shì). Plain 開 kāi is also used for the same things.

hint: a time word, not gāng gāng
note: A time word for 'a moment ago'. Taiwanese more often say 剛剛 gāng gāng, which means the same thing.
A bit more formal or general than plain 學 xué. In casual speech people say 學中文 xué zhōng wén more than 學習中文. MOE also lists xué xi, but Taiwan speech uses xué xí.

hint: formal money unit, spoken is kuài
note: The formal unit of money (in Taiwan, NT dollars). You see and hear it on prices and announcements: 一百元 yī bǎi yuán. In everyday talk Taiwanese say 塊 kuài.

example.english: A cup of coffee is eighty dollars.

note: In Taiwan this is the motor scooter, the most common way to get around: 騎機車 qí jī chē 'ride a scooter'. As slang, 很機車 hěn jī chē describes an annoying, difficult person. On the mainland 機車 means a locomotive.

example.english: I ride my scooter to work.

note: Cooked rice is 飯 fàn. On the mainland 米 also means 'meter'; Taiwan usually says 公尺 gōng chǐ.

example.english: We're out of rice at home.

note: Literally 'see again'. Casually, Taiwanese often say 掰掰 bāi bāi.
Also a noun for sports or exercise, and for a social or political movement. MOE also lists yùn dong, but Taiwan speech normally uses yùn dòng.

hint: lay out the details, e.g. instructions
note: Explaining how or what something is. 解釋 jiě shì leans more toward explaining why. 說明書 shuō míng shū is an instruction manual.

example.english: Let me explain it to you.

note: 洗手 xǐ shǒu 'wash your hands', 洗碗 xǐ wǎn 'do the dishes', 洗衣服 xǐ yī fu 'do the laundry', 洗頭 xǐ tóu 'wash your hair'. 洗澡 xǐ zǎo is 'to shower'.
Goes at the end of a noun phrase: 我最好的朋友之一 'one of my best friends'.

example.trad: 這是我最喜歡的歌之一。
example.simp: 这是我最喜欢的歌之一。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ zuì xǐhuān de gē zhīyī.
example.english: This is one of my favorite songs.

note: Used before a noun (別的東西 bié de dōng xi 'other things') or on its own (還要別的嗎？ 'anything else?'). 'Other people' is usually 別人 bié rén; 其他 qí tā is a bit more formal.
Usually comes as 試試看 shì shi kàn or 試一下 shì yī xià ('give it a try'), or 試穿 shì chuān 'try on clothes'.

example.english: You can give it a try.

gloss: to belong to; to fall under
note: Used for categories, scope or responsibility. For simple ownership people say 是他的 shì tā de 'it's his'.

example.trad: 這不屬於我的工作範圍。
example.simp: 这不属于我的工作范围。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù shǔyú wǒ de gōngzuò fànwéi.
example.english: This isn't part of my job.

note: In everyday Taiwan speech 房間 usually means a bedroom: 回房間 'go to my room'.
A location word, used after a noun: 桌子上面 'on the table'. MOE lists shàng mian with a neutral tone, but Taiwanese usually say shàng miàn.

example.english: The phone is on the table.

note: Formal or written. In everyday Taiwan speech 老公 lǎo gōng is far more common. Taiwan (MOE) says zhàng fū; the mainland says zhàng fu.

hint: inner or collective power, not lì qi
note: MOE gives lì liang; many Taiwanese say lì liàng. Physical strength (as in having no energy left) is usually 力氣 lì qi.

example.trad: 你的話給了我很多力量。
example.simp: 你的话给了我很多力量。
example.pinyin: Nǐ de huà gěi le wǒ hěn duō lìliang.
example.english: Your words gave me a lot of strength.

hint: at the end of a sentence
note: Goes at the end of a sentence to play something down, often together with 只是 or 只有: 只是開玩笑而已 'just joking, that's all'.

hint: both directions, depending on word order
note: 跟…借 gēn … jiè 'borrow from…': 我跟他借錢 'I borrowed money from him'. 借…給 or 借 + person means 'lend': 借我 'lend me'. To give it back is 還 huán.

example.pinyin: Kěyǐ jiè wǒ yī zhī bǐ ma?
example.english: Could you lend me a pen?

note: Often said as 猜猜看 cāi cai kàn 'take a guess'.
Measure word for episodes of TV shows and series: 這部連續劇有二十集 zhè bù lián xù jù yǒu èr shí jí 'this series has twenty episodes'. Also means 'to gather', mostly inside words like 集合 jí hé.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān kàn le sān jí.

note: Used to answer the phone or to call out to someone. MOE gives wèi; mainland dictionaries give wéi for the phone greeting, and in real speech it often comes out rising. As a verb, wèi means 'to feed' (喂奶 wèi nǎi).

example.english: Hello? Who would you like to speak to?

note: Picks out part of a group, often in pairs: 有的人…，有的人… 'some people ..., others ...'.

example.trad: 有的人喜歡，有的人不喜歡。
example.simp: 有的人喜欢，有的人不喜欢。
example.pinyin: Yǒude rén xǐhuān, yǒude rén bù xǐhuān.
example.english: Some people like it, some don't.

note: Mostly heard inside words: 前面 qián miàn, 見面 jiàn miàn 'to meet'; a person's face is 臉 liǎn. Also a measure word for flat things (一面鏡子 yī miàn jìng zi 'a mirror'). 'Noodles' (麵) sounds the same.
Sounds the same as 面 'side / surface'. Common in Taiwan food: 牛肉麵 niú ròu miàn 'beef noodle soup', 炒麵 chǎo miàn 'fried noodles'.

example.english: I want to eat beef noodle soup.

note: Implies that the plan or situation later changed: 我本來要去，可是… 'I was going to go, but ...'.

example.trad: 我本來想去，後來太累了。
example.simp: 我本来想去，后来太累了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ běnlái xiǎng qù, hòulái tài lèi le.
example.english: I wanted to go at first, but then I got too tired.

example.pinyin: Tā bù chéngrèn shì tā zuò de.
example.english: He won't admit he did it.

note: 慢一點 màn yī diǎn 'a bit slower'. 慢慢來 màn màn lái 'take your time'. 慢走 màn zǒu 'take care' is said to a guest who is leaving.

example.english: Take your time, there's no rush.

note: Used both for people stating something and for things that indicate or mean something: 這表示… 'this means ...'.

example.trad: 他沒回答，表示他不同意。
example.simp: 他没回答，表示他不同意。
example.pinyin: Tā méi huídá, biǎoshì tā bù tóngyì.
example.english: He didn't answer, which means he disagrees.

note: 沒想到 méi xiǎng dào means 'didn't expect' or 'surprisingly'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ méi xiǎngdào nǐ huì lái.
example.english: I didn't expect you to come.

note: The noun. 'To have a meeting' is usually 開會 kāi huì.

example.english: What time does the meeting start?

note: Counted with 首 shǒu: 一首歌. 'To sing' is 唱歌 chàng gē.
Measure word for drinks: 一杯水 yī bēi shuǐ 'a glass of water', 兩杯咖啡. The cup itself is 杯子 bēi zi.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yào yī bēi rè chá.
example.english: I'd like a cup of hot tea.

note: The general word for alcoholic drinks. Specific kinds: 啤酒 pí jiǔ 'beer', 紅酒 hóng jiǔ 'red wine'. 喝酒 hē jiǔ means 'to drink (alcohol)'.

example.pinyin: Tā wǎnshang hē le hěn duō jiǔ.
example.english: He drank a lot this evening.

note: Body part + 痛: 頭痛 tóu tòng 'headache', 肚子痛 dù zi tòng 'stomachache'. 好痛！ hǎo tòng 'ouch!'. 痛苦 tòng kǔ is deeper, longer suffering.
Also means 'my family': 家裡有四個人. MOE lists jiā li with a neutral tone, but Taiwanese usually say jiā lǐ.
Often before a noun with 的: 同樣的問題 'the same problem'. In casual speech 一樣 yī yàng is more common.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yě yǒu tóngyàng de wèntí.

note: The Christian God is usually 上帝 shàng dì. Also used in slang: 好神 hǎo shén or 太神了 'amazing / uncanny'.
The everyday word for morning; 上午 shàng wǔ is more formal, like "a.m." in schedules. MOE gives zǎo shang; many Taiwanese say zǎo shàng.

example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang qī diǎn qǐchuáng.
example.english: I get up at seven every morning.

note: Usually paired with 也 yě in the second clause: 即使下雨，我也要去 'even if it rains, I'll still go'. 就算 jiù suàn is the more casual equivalent.

example.pinyin: Jíshǐ hěn lèi, tā yě qù shàngbān.
example.english: Even when he's tired, he still goes to work.

hint: what happened next, in the past
note: Only for past events ('and then later ...'). For the future, use 以後 yǐ hòu or 等一下 děng yī xià.
For answering a question. Replying to a message is usually 回 huí (回訊息 'reply to a message').

example.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu huídá wǒ de wèntí.

note: 有意見 yǒu yì jiàn can also mean 'to have an objection or complaint', so 你有什麼意見？ can sound like 'Got a problem with that?'

example.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng tīngting nǐ de yìjiàn.
example.english: I'd like to hear your opinion.

gloss: to care about; to be concerned
to leave behind; to stay behind
note: MOE lists liú xia with a light 下, but the full tone is common in Taiwan speech. 留下來 liú xià lái means 'to stay (on)'.

example.pinyin: Tā liúxià yī fēng xìn jiù zǒu le.
example.english: He left a letter and went away.

note: Praise for skill: 你好厲害 nǐ hǎo lì hài 'you're amazing!'. Also 'severe, intense': 痛得很厲害 tòng de hěn lì hài 'it hurts badly'. MOE gives full tones (lì hài); the mainland says lì hai.

hint: a bit more formal than cháng cháng
note: Everyday speech often uses 常常 cháng cháng or just 常 cháng.

gloss: no need to; don't have to
note: Spoken bú yòng (不 becomes bú before a 4th tone). Also a polite reply: 不用了 'no thanks', 不用謝 bù yòng xiè 'no need to thank me'.

example.english: You don't need to wait for me.

note: Before a verb it can mean 'hard to': 不好找 'hard to find'. 不好意思 bù hǎo yì si means 'sorry / excuse me'.

gloss: to pretend; to pack in; to install
hint: fake it, or put something in
note: Covers 'pretend' (別裝了 bié zhuāng le 'stop pretending'), 'put into a container' (裝水) and 'install' (裝冷氣 'install an air conditioner').

example.pinyin: Bié zhuāng le, wǒ zhīdào shì nǐ.
example.english: Stop pretending, I know it was you.

hint: to open a list of points
note: Starts a sequence of points, often followed by 然後 or 再來. Compare 先 xiān 'do first, beforehand'.

example.english: First of all, you need to be patient.

note: 年輕人 nián qīng rén means 'young people'.
Most often used when you realize something: 原來如此 yuán lái rú cǐ 'I see'. Also 'original, former': 原來的地方 'the original place'.

example.english: My parents are against us getting married.

gloss: no way; not OK; not allowed
note: The opposite of 行 xíng 'OK'. Also 'no good at' (我數學不行 'I'm bad at math') and, after an adjective, 'extremely' (累得不行 'exhausted').
The opposite is 髒 zāng 'dirty'. 乾 here is gān 'dry', not qián. MOE gives full tones (gān jìng); the mainland says gān jing.

example.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ fángjiān dǎsǎo gānjìng le.

gloss: in fact; as a matter of fact
hint: formal; the facts are, contrary to belief
note: Fairly formal. Everyday speech usually says 其實 qí shí 'actually'. Compare 實際上 shí jì shàng 'in reality'.

example.pinyin: Shìshíshàng, tā zǎo jiù zhīdào le.
example.english: In fact, he knew long ago.

hint: mail, a message or a gift
note: In messages, 收到 alone means 'got it / received'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ shōudào wǒ de xùnxí le ma?

note: Also used playfully: 你好討厭喔！ 'You're so annoying!' (teasing).
'To have a dream' is 做夢 zuò mèng; 夢到 mèng dào means 'to dream about'.

example.trad: 我昨天晚上做了一個很奇怪的夢。
example.simp: 我昨天晚上做了一个很奇怪的梦。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān wǎnshang zuò le yī ge hěn qíguài de mèng.
example.english: I had a strange dream last night.

example.pinyin: Hǎo qíguài, tā zěnme hái méi lái?
example.english: That's weird, why isn't he here yet?

hint: interesting or amusing, not 'fun to do'
note: Common in everyday Taiwan speech (好有趣). For activities that are fun, Taiwanese usually say 好玩 hǎo wán; 有意思 yǒu yì si sounds more mainland.

gloss: to be afraid of; to fear
hint: short everyday word, takes an object
note: Also 'to worry that': 我怕來不及 'I'm afraid we won't make it'. Compare 害怕 hài pà 'scared'.

hint: a small group or a set
note: Also a measure word for sets and groups: 一組 yī zǔ 'one set / one group'. As a verb it means 'to form': 組隊 zǔ duì 'form a team'.

gloss: to pass by; to go through
note: As a noun it means 'what happened, the course of events': 事情的經過.

example.pinyin: Wǒ měi tiān dōu jīngguò zhè jiā diàn.
example.english: I pass this shop every day.

gloss: good-looking; nice; good (to watch or read)
hint: looks good; also a good show or book
note: For people and things: 你穿這樣很好看 'you look good in that'. For movies and books: 這部電影很好看 zhè bù diàn yǐng hěn hǎo kàn 'this movie is good'. The opposite is 難看 nán kàn 'ugly'.
Formal-sounding. In everyday speech 最後 zuì hòu is more common.

example.english: In the end he still gave up.

note: MOE reads 幾 as jī here; in 'how many' it is jǐ. Some speakers say jǐ hū.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jīhū měi tiān dōu hē kāfēi.
example.english: I drink coffee almost every day.

note: With numbers it means 'about': 大概十分鐘 'about ten minutes'. As a noun, 'the general idea'.

example.pinyin: Tā dàgài bù huì lái le.

note: Taiwan (MOE) reads 識 as shì here; the mainland says yì shí. 意識到 yì shì dào means 'to realize'.

example.trad: 他突然意識到自己錯了。
example.simp: 他突然意识到自己错了。
example.pinyin: Tā túrán yìshì dào zìjǐ cuò le.
example.english: He suddenly realized he was wrong.

example.pinyin: Zhè fùjìn yǒu biànlì shāngdiàn ma?
example.english: Is there a convenience store around here?

note: 好玩嗎？ hǎo wán ma 'was it fun?'. 有趣 yǒu qù is 'interesting'. MOE also lists hào wán 'fond of play', which is rare.
Very common as 沒必要 méi bì yào 'there's no need'. Compare 必須 bì xū 'must'.

example.english: There's no need to go that far.

note: 興 is xìng here (mood, interest). The other reading xīng means 'to rise, prosper', as in 興奮 xīng fèn 'excited'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ duì yīnyuè hěn yǒu xìngqù.

note: In casual speech people usually just say 對 duì 'right'.

example.english: Doing it this way is right.

note: 'To sing (songs)' is usually 唱歌 chàng gē.

example.english: He's still being treated in the hospital.

hint: formal; as opposed to in theory
note: Fairly formal. Everyday speech usually says 其實 qí shí 'actually'. Compare 事實上 shì shí shàng 'in fact'.

example.trad: 實際上，事情沒那麼簡單。
example.simp: 实际上，事情没那么简单。
example.english: In reality, it's not that simple.
There are a lot of reporters outside.

hint: location, the front side; up ahead
note: 'In front (of)' and 'up ahead': 在前面 zài qián miàn. The opposite is 後面 hòu miàn 'behind'. Taiwan (MOE) keeps the full tone on 面.

example.english: The convenience store is just up ahead.

note: Casually, 'to be in jail' is 坐牢 zuò láo or 被關 bèi guān 'locked up'.

example.pinyin: Tā zài jiānyù lǐ dāi le sān nián.
example.english: He spent three years in prison.

hint: agreeing: 'it's true that…'; not què shí
note: 的 is dí here, not the particle de; in 目的 mù dì 'purpose' it is dì.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn díquè hěn hǎochī.

note: 種 zhǒng means 'kind, type'; as 'to plant' it is zhòng. Casually 那 is often said nèi: nèi zhǒng.

example.pinyin: Wǒ bù xǐhuān nà zhǒng rén.
example.english: I don't like that kind of person.

note: MOE also lists shí zai with a light tone. As an adjective it means honest, down-to-earth: 他人很實在.

hint: right by the side of something
note: Goes after the thing: 我家旁邊 wǒ jiā páng biān 'next to my place'. 坐我旁邊 'sit next to me'.
Counts thin, flat things: 一片麵包 'a slice of bread', 一片葉子 'a leaf'. Also means 'film' in 影片. MOE also lists piān, used in a few colloquial words but rare in Taiwan.

example.pinyin: Wǒ chī le liǎng piàn miànbāo.
example.english: I ate two slices of bread.

note: Counts songs and poems: 一首歌 yī shǒu gē 'a song'. It also means 'head / first' in words like 首先 shǒu xiān 'first of all'.
Introduces what happens if the first part isn't done. In casual speech Taiwanese usually say 不然 bù rán instead.

example.pinyin: Yào chuān wàitào, fǒuzé huì gǎnmào.
example.english: Wear a jacket, or else you'll catch a cold.

note: A more formal word for 'still'. In everyday speech people usually say 還 hái or 還是 hái shì.
MOE also lists a reading lù, used only in a few place names; for the number it is always liù.

example.english: I get off work at six.

note: Some older speakers say qí before a 4th tone (七次), but most Taiwanese keep qī.

example.pinyin: Yī ge xīngqí yǒu qī tiān.

note: A lucky number (from a Cantonese pun with 發 'to prosper'; in Mandarin bā and fā don't sound alike). In chat, 88 means 'bye-bye'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang bā diǎn qǐchuáng.
example.english: I get up at eight every morning.

note: Sounds like 久 jiǔ 'long-lasting', so it is a lucky number for love and long life.

example.english: I get off work at nine.

note: Builds the numbers up to 99: 十一 shí yī (11), 二十 èr shí (20). Listen for the tone: shí (ten) and sì (four) can sound alike in Taiwan accents.
Fills gaps inside numbers: 一百零五 (105). Also means small or scattered: 零錢 líng qián 'small change'. MOE lists a rare historical reading lián.

example.pinyin: Zǒnggòng yī bǎi líng wǔ kuài.
example.english: That's a hundred and five dollars in total.

hint: true to reality, not made up
note: Describes something that actually happened or is not fake: 真實的故事 'a true story'. Compare 真的 zhēn de 'really' and 真正 zhēn zhèng 'genuine'.
Usually with 離 lí: 離這裡很近 'close to here'. The opposite is 遠 yuǎn. 附近 fù jìn means 'nearby / the area around'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā lí gōngsī hěn jìn.
example.english: My home is close to the office.

note: Taiwan (MOE) keeps the full tone hòu miàn; the mainland often says hòu mian. The opposite is 前面 qián miàn 'in front'.
Taiwan writes 想像; the mainland usually writes 想象. Same pronunciation.

example.pinyin: Hěn nán xiǎngxiàng tā huì zhèyàng.
example.english: It's hard to imagine he'd act like this.

note: Often shortened to 男友 nán yǒu. 男生 nán shēng is 'a guy' in general.

hint: vehicles only; more formal than tái
note: Counts cars, buses, bikes and scooters: 一輛車 yī liàng chē. In Taiwan speech 台 tái is also very common for vehicles (一台車).

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu liǎng liàng chē.

note: Used for amounts, times and limits, and also for overtaking: 超過前面的車 'pass the car in front'.

example.english: He goes to training every day.

note: As a measure word it counts bites or mouthfuls (吃一口 chī yī kǒu 'take a bite') and family members (一家四口 yī jiā sì kǒu 'a family of four'). For the body part people usually say 嘴 zuǐ or 嘴巴; 口 also appears in 門口 mén kǒu 'doorway' and 出口 chū kǒu 'exit'.
After a verb it means 'all gone': 錢花光了 qián huā guāng le 'the money's all spent'. Before a verb it means 'just / only': 光說不做 'all talk, no action'.

example.pinyin: Fángjiān lǐ yīdiǎn guāng dōu méiyǒu.
example.english: There's no light at all in the room.

note: Often shortened to 女友 nǚ yǒu. 女生 nǚ shēng is 'a girl, a woman' in general.
大自然 dà zì rán is 'nature' (the outdoors). MOE also lists zì ran for 'relaxed, unforced' (表情很自然), but Taiwanese generally say zì rán.

example.pinyin: Shíjiān jiǔ le zìrán jiù hǎo le.
example.english: Give it time and it'll get better on its own.

note: The reason someone gives for doing something. 原因 yuán yīn is the cause of why something happened.
Usually heard in words: 西邊 xī biān 'the west side', 西方 xī fāng 'the West'. Not the same word as 東西 dōng xi 'thing'.

example.english: The sun sets in the west.

hint: wrap up; also a handbag or a pack
note: Also a measure word for packs: 一包衛生紙 'a pack of tissues'. For a bag, Taiwanese usually say 包包 bāo bāo (handbag) or 背包 bēi bāo (backpack), and 打包 dǎ bāo means to box up leftovers to take home.

example.pinyin: Kěyǐ bāng wǒ bāo qǐlái ma?
example.english: Could you wrap it up for me?

note: Read jià in 放假 fàng jià 'to have time off' and 請假 qǐng jià 'to ask for leave'. 真的假的？ zhēn de jiǎ de 'Seriously?' is very common in Taiwan.
A more formal way of saying 好像 hǎo xiàng, which is what people usually say in conversation.
Adds emphasis, often with exaggeration: 簡直太好了 'just too good', 簡直不敢相信 'simply can't believe it'.
Counted with 條 tiáo: 一條魚 yī tiáo yú. Fish is eaten at Lunar New Year because 魚 sounds like 餘 yú 'surplus' (年年有餘).
Also 'stuck' or 'laggy': 卡住了 'it's stuck', 電腦很卡 'the computer is laggy'. MOE gives qiǎ for 'wedged / stuck', but Taiwanese usually say kǎ.
Most often 瘋了 fēng le 'gone crazy'. 瘋狂 fēng kuáng is more 'wild, frenzied'.

gloss: to take care of; to look after
note: MOE lists both zhào gù and the lighter zhào gu; Taiwanese normally say zhào gù. 謝謝你的照顧 'thanks for looking after me' is a common polite phrase.

example.english: She stays home looking after the kids.

example.pinyin: Wǒ huì yīzhí zài nǐ shēnbiān.
example.english: I'll always be by your side.

note: Common in 記住 jì zhù 'to memorize' and 記下來 jì xià lái 'to write down'. 'To remember' in the sense of still having it in memory is usually 記得 jì de.
Used to address an audience or a group directly, like 'ladies and gentlemen'. In everyday speech 大家 dà jiā is more common.

example.english: Everyone, please be quiet for a moment.

note: In Taiwan, plain 肉 usually means pork; other meats are named: 牛肉 niú ròu 'beef', 雞肉 jī ròu 'chicken'. Many Taiwanese avoid beef for traditional or religious reasons.
Taiwan (MOE) keeps the full tone wèi zhì; the mainland often says wèi zhi. For a seat, Taiwanese also say 位子 wèi zi.

example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ chuán wèizhì gěi wǒ ma?
example.english: Can you send me your location?

note: An adverb that goes before the verb. Compare 明顯 míng xiǎn 'obvious', which describes something.

example.english: He obviously doesn't want to go.

gloss: can only; have no choice but
note: 只 'only' + 能 'can'. Goes before a verb to say it's the only option left.

example.pinyin: Méi chē le, wǒmen zhǐnéng zǒulù.
example.english: There are no more buses, so we can only walk.

note: In daily Taiwan speech people just say 車 chē. A scooter is 機車 jī chē.

example.english: He works at a car company.

note: Usually followed by 都 dōu later in the sentence: 無論如何都要去 'have to go no matter what'. 不管 bù guǎn means the same and is more casual.

example.pinyin: Wúlùn rúhé, wǒ dōu huì qù.

hint: art, with a pen or brush
note: Also a noun, 'a painting': 一幅畫 yī fú huà. 畫畫 huà huà means 'to draw pictures'.
A slightly formal 'quite / rather'; casual speech uses 很 hěn or 蠻 mán. 相當於 xiāng dāng yú means 'equivalent to'.
喝茶 hē chá 'drink tea'. Taiwan is famous for oolong 烏龍茶 wū lóng chá and bubble tea 珍珠奶茶 zhēn zhū nǎi chá.

example.pinyin: Yào bù yào hē bēi chá?
example.english: Would you like a cup of tea?

note: Counted with 張 zhāng: 一張床. 起床 qǐ chuáng means 'to get up'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yào shàng chuáng shuìjiào le.

note: Taiwan (MOE) reads it yī huǐ; the mainland says yí huìr (一會兒). Taiwanese more often use 一下 yī xià for 'a moment'.

example.english: It'll be fine in a little while.

note: Two uses: 'even though' (more formal than 雖然 suī rán), and before a verb 'feel free to': 有問題儘管問 'feel free to ask'.

example.pinyin: Jǐnguǎn hěn lèi, tā háishì lái le.
example.english: Even though he was tired, he still came.

gloss: to arrive at; to come to
note: Not in the MOE dictionary as a word; it's simply 來 'come' + 到 'arrive', read lái dào.
Sounds the same as 反映 fǎn yìng 'to reflect; to report (a problem)', which Taiwanese use a lot, e.g. 跟老闆反映 'bring it up with the boss'.
One written Chinese character, often loosely 'word'. Also 'handwriting': 你的字很漂亮. A word as a unit of meaning is 詞 cí.

example.english: How do you say this character?

note: Taiwan fruit words: 芒果 máng guǒ 'mango', 鳳梨 fèng lí 'pineapple' (mainland 菠蘿), 西瓜 xī guā 'watermelon'.
Taiwan standard (MOE) reading is xiě, as in 流血 liú xiě 'to bleed'. The other reading xuè is the literary one, and the mainland standard in most compounds.
Also in 現金 xiàn jīn 'cash' and 金色 jīn sè 'gold color'. A common surname too.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo xiàngliàn shì jīn de.

note: For people you bump into and for problems or situations: 遇到問題 'run into a problem'. To arrange to meet someone is 見面. 碰到 pèng dào means the same and is just as common in Taiwan.

example.english: I ran into my teacher on the way.

note: Often shortened to 哥 gē, which is also used to address an older guy. Younger brother is 弟弟 dì di.

example.pinyin: Wǒ gēge bǐ wǒ dà sān suì.
example.english: My brother is three years older than me.

note: For stopping someone else or preventing something. To stop doing something yourself is 停 tíng or 停止 tíng zhǐ.
Counted with 家 jiā: 這家店 'this shop'. Common in compounds: 書店 'bookstore', 飯店 'hotel'.

hint: lend a hand; not before a person
note: Often stands alone (需要幫忙嗎？) or goes before a verb (幫忙拿一下 'help carry this'), and splits around other words: 幫我一個忙 'do me a favor'. To help a person directly, use 幫: 幫我.
恭喜！ alone, or 恭喜你 gōng xǐ nǐ 'congratulations (to you)'. The Lunar New Year greeting is 恭喜發財 gōng xǐ fā cái.
Counts sentences and things said: 一句話 'one sentence', 說兩句 'say a few words'. The rare literary reading gōu is not used in speech.

example.pinyin: Tā yī jù huà dōu méi shuō.
example.english: He didn't say a single word.

note: Measure word for groups of people or animals: 一群人 'a crowd', 一群鳥 'a flock of birds'. A group chat is 群組 qún zǔ.

example.english: There's a crowd of people outside.

note: Measure word for pairs: shoes, socks, chopsticks, eyes (一雙鞋, 一雙筷子). Couples and matched sets use 對 duì (一對夫妻). The rare reading shuàng is not used in speech.

example.pinyin: Wǒ mǎile yī shuāng xīn xié.
example.english: I bought a new pair of shoes.

note: In Taiwan you call out 老闆 to any shop or stall owner; a woman owner is 老闆娘 lǎo bǎn niáng.

example.english: Excuse me (boss), how much is this?

note: Mostly heard in 跳舞 tiào wǔ 'to dance' (lit. 'jump dance'); also 一支舞 'a dance'.
More formal than 讓 ràng or 可以 kě yǐ; common in rules: 不允許 'not allowed'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ mā bù yǔnxǔ wǒ yǎng gǒu.
example.english: My mom won't let me have a dog.

note: Often 值得 + verb: 值得去 'worth going'. MOE gives a light 得 (zhí de), but many Taiwanese say zhí dé.

example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū hěn zhíde kàn.
example.english: This book is really worth reading.

note: Counts sounds and utterances: 叫一聲 'give a shout', 說一聲 'let someone know'. The full word for sound or voice is 聲音 shēng yīn.

example.pinyin: Dàole gēn wǒ shuō yī shēng.
example.english: Let me know when you get there.

note: 跟…道歉 gēn … dào qiàn 'apologize to…'. The apology itself is 對不起 duì bu qǐ or 不好意思 bù hǎo yì si.
The casual word for 'wife' (老公 lǎo gōng is 'husband'); 太太 tài tai is the polite word, especially for someone else's wife, and 妻子 qī zi is formal. MOE gives lǎo po, but many Taiwanese say lǎo pó.

example.english: My wife is a great cook.

note: Means the same as 那裡 and is very common in Taiwan, with a full tone on biān. Mainland speech often has nà bian or 那兒. 'Over here' is 這邊 zhè biān.
A location word used after a noun: 桌子下面 'under the table'. Also 'next / the following': 下面我們… 'next, we…'. You may also hear a light xià mian.

example.english: The keys are under the table.

note: 怪怪的 guài guài de 'a bit off' is very common in Taiwan. As a verb, 'to blame': 不要怪我 'don't blame me'. 難怪 nán guài means 'no wonder'.

example.english: He's acting a bit weird today.

note: Polyphone: shǔ is 'to count' (數到三 'count to three'). Read shù it means 'number' (數字 shù zì, 分數 fēn shù 'score').
Formal; used in speeches and announcements: 再次感謝 'thanks again'. In conversation people say 再一次 or just 再 zài.

gloss: to meet up; to see each other
note: Takes no object; use 跟 gēn: 跟朋友見面 gēn péng yǒu jiàn miàn 'meet up with friends'.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen hǎo jiǔ méi jiànmiàn le.
example.english: We haven't seen each other in ages.

note: The Taiwan word for an online video (mainland: 視頻). A movie at the cinema is 電影 diàn yǐng.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zài kàn māo de yǐngpiàn.

note: Asks only about lengths of time: 要等多久？ 'how long do we wait?'. 沒多久 means 'not long (after)'.

example.english: How long have you been in Taiwan?

example.pinyin: Nǐ míngtiān yào qù tóupiào ma?
example.english: Are you going to vote tomorrow?

note: Often said as 比如說 bǐ rú shuō; 比方說 bǐ fāng shuō is also very common in Taiwan. 例如 lì rú is more formal.
You 'eat' medicine: 吃藥 chī yào 'to take medicine'. A pharmacy in Taiwan is 藥局 yào jú.
生病 shēng bìng 'to get sick', 看病 kàn bìng 'to see a doctor'. 他病了 'he's sick'.

example.pinyin: Tā de bìng hǎo le ma?
example.english: Has he gotten over his illness?

note: 壓力很大 'very stressed (lots of pressure)'.

example.english: Work has been really stressful lately.

note: 差不多了 chà bu duō le 'almost done; that'll do'. 差不多五點 'around five'. MOE reads the 不 lightly (chà bu duō); many people say chà bù duō.
Describes a person who puts in real effort. 你認真的嗎？ 'Are you serious?' A serious problem or illness is 嚴重 yán zhòng.

example.english: He pays close attention in class.

note: In everyday Taiwan speech 腳 often covers the whole leg too; strictly, the leg is 腿 tuǐ. The literary reading jué is rare.

hint: unit of meaning, not one character
note: A word as a unit of meaning, often two characters: 朋友 is one 詞 but two 字 zì. 歌詞 gē cí means 'lyrics'.
More formal than 停 tíng; used for activities, plans and machines. To say 'stop it!' people use 不要 or 別.

example.english: He decided to stop the plan.

note: Same meaning as 忘 wàng. 忘了 wàng le is the most common casual way to say 'forgot'.

example.english: I forgot to bring my wallet.

note: In Taiwan a computer file is 檔案 dǎng àn; 文件 means documents or paperwork (the mainland also uses it for computer files). Counted with 份 fèn.
Hugely common in Taiwan: 超好吃 'super tasty', 超累 'so tired'. The original verb meaning is 'to exceed / overtake' (超車 'overtake', 超過 'exceed').

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā de niúròumiàn chāo hǎochī!
example.english: This place's beef noodles are super good!

gloss: to keep (someone) company; to go with
note: 陪我 péi wǒ 'keep me company'. 陪小孩 péi xiǎo hái 'spend time with the kids'. 陪你去 péi nǐ qù 'go with you'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ péi nǐ qù kàn yīshēng.
example.english: I'll go to the doctor with you.

note: The opposite of 裡面 lǐ miàn 'inside'. In fast speech it is often wài mian, and Taiwanese also say 外頭 wài tou.
Counted with 條: 一條街 yī tiáo jiē. 逛街 guàng jiē means to go shopping or stroll around the shops. A road or main city street is usually 路 lù.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo jiē wǎnshang hěn rènao.
example.english: This street is lively at night.

note: 坐船 zuò chuán means to go by boat. 暈船 yūn chuán means seasick.

example.english: How long does it take by boat?

note: Very common in Taiwan, as are 小孩子 xiǎo hái zi and 小朋友 xiǎo péng yǒu (also used to address children). Compare 孩子 hái zi.
Polyphone: read chòng it means blunt or harsh (他說話很衝 tā shuō huà hěn chòng 'he talks rudely') or 'toward'.

example.pinyin: Tā yī tīngdào jiù chōng chūqù le.
example.english: As soon as he heard it, he rushed out.

note: Taiwan writes 身分 (MOE); the mainland writes 身份. 身分證 shēn fèn zhèng is the national ID card.

example.english: I forgot to bring my ID card.

note: Also a suffix for a person with a bad habit: 小氣鬼 xiǎo qì guǐ 'cheapskate', 膽小鬼 dǎn xiǎo guǐ 'coward'. 鬼月 guǐ yuè is Ghost Month, a big deal in Taiwan.
For spicy food, use 辣 là. 熱 also means 'to heat up': 熱一下 rè yī xià 'warm it up'.
安靜一點！ ān jìng yī diǎn 'be quiet!'. The opposite is 吵 chǎo 'noisy'.
Used after a person: 在我面前 zài wǒ miàn qián 'in front of me'. 前面 qián miàn is the general 'in front; ahead'.

example.english: Don't smoke in front of the kids.

note: 掛號 guà hào means to register at a clinic or send registered mail. In slang, 掛了 guà le can mean 'died' or 'crashed'.

example.english: I'm going to hang up now.

note: MOE also lists bì as a variant reading, but bī is what people say.
Also in 反正 fǎn zhèng 'anyway', 相反 xiāng fǎn 'opposite' and 反對 fǎn duì 'to oppose'. MOE's other readings fān and fàn are rare and literary.

example.english: You've got your shirt on inside out.

note: Usually deeper or longer suffering than 痛 tòng 'to hurt; to ache'. Also a noun: 'suffering'.
Often in the forms 做得到 zuò de dào 'can do it' and 做不到 zuò bu dào 'can't do it'.

gloss: to lie to; to cheat; to trick
note: 騙人！ piàn rén on its own means 'You're lying! / No way!'. 騙子 piàn zi is a liar or con artist.

hint: polite everyday word; also a title
note: 我太太 wǒ tài tai 'my wife' is the polite everyday word in Taiwan; 老婆 lǎo po is more intimate and casual. After a surname it means 'Mrs.': 王太太 'Mrs. Wang'.

example.pinyin: Wáng tàitai shì wǒmen de línjū.

note: Used in the pattern 不是 A，而是 B (bù shì A, ér shì B) 'not A, but (rather) B'. It corrects the first part instead of contrasting like 但是 dàn shì.

example.trad: 不是我不想去，而是沒時間。
example.simp: 不是我不想去，而是没时间。
example.pinyin: Bùshì wǒ bù xiǎng qù, érshì méi shíjiān.
example.english: It's not that I don't want to go, it's that I don't have time.

note: 受傷 shòu shāng is 'to get hurt'. 傷心 shāng xīn is 'sad; heartbroken'. For 'it hurts / it aches', say 痛 tòng.

example.pinyin: Tā de shāng hái méi hǎo.

note: A more formal or literary version of 找 zhǎo. Common in songs, news and abstract things like dreams or answers.

example.trad: 他還在尋找自己的夢想。
example.simp: 他还在寻找自己的梦想。
example.pinyin: Tā hái zài xúnzhǎo zìjǐ de mèngxiǎng.
example.english: He's still searching for his dream.
This website is easy to use.

note: 醒了 xǐng le 'woke up; is awake'. 叫醒 jiào xǐng 'to wake someone up'. Getting out of bed is 起床 qǐ chuáng.
In speech it is often něi ge, and 哪一個 nǎ yī ge is also common. 個 is light here, like 這個 zhè ge.

example.english: Which one do you like better?

note: MOE reads 場 as cháng here; many Taiwanese say shì chǎng, as the mainland does. 菜市場 cài shì cháng is the traditional wet market.

example.pinyin: Wǒ mā měitiān qù shìcháng mǎi cài.
example.english: My mom goes to the market every day to buy groceries.

note: 丟垃圾 diū lè sè means 'throw away trash'; taking the trash out to the garbage truck is 倒垃圾 dào lè sè. 丟臉 diū liǎn means 'embarrassing; lose face'. Losing a game is 輸 shū.
Common phrases: 交作業 jiāo zuò yè 'hand in homework', 交朋友 jiāo péng yǒu 'make friends', 交女朋友 jiāo nǚ péng yǒu 'get a girlfriend', 交給 jiāo gěi 'hand over to'.
Stronger than 喜歡 'to like': it means really savoring something. Also a noun, 'enjoyment'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xiǎngshòu xiànzài de shēnghuó.
example.english: I really enjoy my life now.

note: More formal than 每 měi except in set phrases: 各位 gè wèi 'everyone (polite address)', 各種 gè zhǒng 'all kinds of', 各付各的 gè fù gè de 'each pays their own'.

gloss: to do one's utmost; to use up
note: Mostly heard in 盡力 jìn lì 'do one's best' and 盡量 jìn liàng 'as much as possible' (also written 儘量 jǐn liàng, a reading many Taiwanese use).
Polyphone: read xǐng it means to reflect on oneself, as in 反省 fǎn xǐng. Putting money in the bank is 存 cún.

example.pinyin: Zhèyàng kěyǐ shěng hěn duō qián.
example.english: This way you can save a lot of money.

note: In everyday Taiwan speech, 男生 nán shēng is the usual word for a boy or guy, and 男孩子 nán hái zi is also common.

example.pinyin: Nàge xiǎo nánhái pǎo de hǎo kuài.
example.english: That little boy runs so fast.

note: 搬家 bān jiā 'to move house'. 搬東西 bān dōng xi 'to carry things'. 搬到台北 'move to Taipei'.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen xià ge yuè yào bānjiā.

gloss: for; on behalf of; to replace
note: As a preposition it works like 幫 bāng or 為 wèi: 替我謝謝他 tì wǒ xiè xie tā 'thank him for me'. As a verb it means to take someone's place.
Counted with 張: 一張圖. 地圖 dì tú is a map. Online, 圖 is any image.
Takes an object: 適合你 shì hé nǐ 'suits you'. The adjective 合適 hé shì 'suitable' means much the same: 很合適 hěn hé shì.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu hěn shìhé nǐ.

hint: a life to save or lose
note: Also in 要命 yào mìng 'terribly; deadly', 算命 suàn mìng 'fortune-telling' and 拼命 pīn mìng 'with all one's might'. Compare 生命 shēng mìng (being alive) and 生活 shēng huó (daily life).
開 kāi alone also covers driving: 開快一點 'drive faster'. Riding a scooter or bike is 騎 qí.
Also a noun: a notice or notification (手機通知 shǒu jī tōng zhī 'phone notification').

example.pinyin: Yǒu xiāoxí wǒ zài tōngzhī nǐ.
example.english: I'll let you know when there's news.

gloss: to shine on; to photograph; according to
note: 照鏡子 zhào jìng zi 'look in the mirror', 拍照 pāi zhào 'take photos', 照你說的做 zhào nǐ shuō de zuò 'do as you say'. Also in 照顧 zhào gù 'take care of'.

example.english: She keeps looking in the mirror.

note: Compare 生活 shēng huó (daily life) and 生命 shēng mìng (being alive).

gloss: please (I beg you); to ask a favor
note: Very common in Taiwan. On its own, 拜託！ bài tuō can also mean 'Oh, come on!' (disbelief or annoyance).

gloss: poor; bad; to be short of
note: Also 'short of': 還差一個人 hái chà yī ge rén 'still one person short'; 差不多 chà bu duō 'about the same'. Other readings: chā in 差別 chā bié 'difference', chāi in 出差 chū chāi 'business trip'.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiā cāntīng de fúwù hěn chà.
example.english: The service at this restaurant is bad.

note: The drink version of 好吃 hǎo chī. 不好喝 bù hǎo hē 'doesn't taste good'.

example.pinyin: Zhè bēi zhēnzhū nǎichá hǎo hǎohē!
example.english: This bubble tea is so good!
How old are you this year?

gloss: to sleep; to go to bed
note: 覺 is jiào here ('a sleep'); in 覺得 jué de it is jué. It splits apart: 睡午覺 shuì wǔ jiào 'take a nap'.
Polyphone: read zàng for a storehouse or Tibet (西藏 Xī zàng). To hide yourself, people usually say 躲 duǒ.

example.pinyin: Nǐ bǎ qián cáng zài nǎlǐ?
example.english: Where did you hide the money?

note: Literally 'not right' (bù + duì). Also used to correct yourself mid-sentence: 不對，是明天 'no wait, it's tomorrow'. Spoken bú duì (tone sandhi).
Also means 'popular, famous': 他現在很紅 'he's really popular now'. MOE also lists a rare literary reading gōng (needlework).
三樓 sān lóu is 'third floor'; 樓上 'upstairs', 樓下 'downstairs', 大樓 'building'. 一樓 is the ground floor (US-style counting).

example.english: I live on the fifth floor.

note: Short form of 有時候 yǒu shí hòu, which is more common in casual speech.
Literally 'ten parts out of ten'. Sounds more formal than 很 hěn or 非常 fēi cháng. Don't confuse with 十分鐘 'ten minutes'.
Taiwan says xīng qí; the mainland says xīng qī. Days: 星期一 'Monday' ... 星期天/星期日 'Sunday'. 禮拜 lǐ bài is a common casual alternative in Taiwan.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xià xīngqí yào qù Táiběi.
example.english: I'm going to Taipei next week.

gloss: to receive; to collect; to put away
hint: one syllable; take in, or put away
note: Common uses: 收錢 'take payment', 收好 'put away safely', 收衣服 'bring in the laundry'. 收到 shōu dào means 'to have received' (mail, a message).

example.pinyin: Lǎobǎn bù shōu wǒ de qián.
example.english: The owner won't take my money.

gloss: to rest; to take a break
note: Taiwan (MOE) says xiū xí with a full second tone; the mainland says xiū xi.

example.pinyin: Nǐ lèi le jiù xiūxí yīxià.
example.english: If you're tired, take a rest.

note: Before a verb it means 'carelessly, at random': 不要亂說 'don't talk nonsense', 亂丟 'throw anywhere'.
Short for 昨天晚上 zuó tiān wǎn shang, which is more common in casual speech.

example.english: I didn't sleep well last night.

hint: a category; more formal than zhǒng
note: Often used like a measure word: 這類電影 'this kind of movie'. In compounds: 人類 'humankind', 分類 'to sort'. 種 zhǒng is the everyday 'kind'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ bù xǐhuān zhè lèi diànyǐng.
example.english: I don't like this kind of movie.

note: Also 'secretly': 偷看 'to peek', 偷偷 tōu tōu 'sneakily'. 小偷 xiǎo tōu is 'thief'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ de jiǎotàchē bèi tōu le.

note: Somewhat formal. Casually people say 請 qǐng or 約 yuē ('ask out, make plans with').

example.english: He invited me to the wedding.

hint: inner feelings about something; not gǎn jué
note: As a noun: one's feelings about something. As a verb: to feel or experience (感受一下 'get a feel for it'). 感覺 gǎn jué is the more everyday 'feeling'.

hint: days of one's life; a set date
note: 過日子 guò rì zi 'to get by, live one's life'; 好日子 'a lucky day (for an event)'. MOE also lists rì zǐ with a full tone.
氣死了 'so angry', 生氣 shēng qì 'to be angry'. Also means air or gas, as in 空氣 kōng qì 'air' and 天氣 tiān qì 'weather'.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ wǒ qì sǐ le.

note: MOE lists both fāng xiàng and a lighter fāng xiang; Taiwan speech keeps the full tone.
Physical injury, but also hurt feelings: 我很受傷 'I'm hurt'.
Also a verb: 公司規定… 'company rules say…'.

hint: as a rule, most of the time

example.english: I usually get up at seven.

note: Literally 'add fuel'. Shouted to encourage or cheer someone on. Also literal: 去加油 'go get gas'.

example.english: You've got an exam tomorrow. Good luck!

note: Common pairs: 犯錯 'make a mistake', 犯法 'break the law', 犯人 'prisoner'.

example.pinyin: Měi ge rén dōu huì fàncuò.

note: Used for things on the head, face or hands: 戴眼鏡 'wear glasses', 戴口罩 'wear a mask'. Clothes and shoes take 穿 chuān. Sounds the same as 帶 dài 'to bring'.

example.pinyin: Wàimiàn hěn lěng, dài màozi ba.
example.english: It's cold out, wear a hat.

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xiǎngniàn wǒ de jiārén.

note: Taiwan (MOE) says cōng míng with a full tone; the mainland says cōng ming.
車票 'train/bus ticket', 電影票 'movie ticket', 投票 tóu piào 'to vote'. Counted with 張 zhāng. MOE's other reading piāo is literary and rare.
的 is read dì here (as in 目的地 'destination'), not the particle de.

example.trad: 你來這裡的目的是什麼？
example.simp: 你来这里的目的是什么？
example.pinyin: Nǐ lái zhèlǐ de mùdì shì shénme?
example.english: What's your purpose in coming here?

note: Often 秒鐘 miǎo zhōng. Slang 秒殺 'sold out in seconds'.
With a clause it usually means 'suspect that…' (我懷疑他在說謊); with a thing it can mean 'doubt' (懷疑自己 'doubt yourself').
For a short person, use 矮 ǎi, not 低. As a verb: 低頭 'lower one's head'.
Pattern 一旦…就… 'once X happens, then Y'. Spoken yí dàn (tone sandhi of 一).

example.english: Once you start, you can't stop.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yào bù yào hē kāfēi?

note: Emphatic 'how' in exclamations, a bit literary; casual speech uses 多 or 好: 好漂亮！ MOE gives duó me, but most Taiwanese say duō me.

example.pinyin: Nǐ bù zhīdào wǒ duōme xiǎng nǐ.
example.english: You don't know how much I miss you.

note: Also an adjective ('difficult'), but 難 nán is the everyday 'hard'. MOE gives kùn nan; many Taiwanese say kùn nán.

example.pinyin: Yǒu kùnnan jiù gēn wǒ shuō.
example.english: If you run into trouble, tell me.

note: Goes before an adjective or verb: 越來越冷 'colder and colder'. Not in MOE as a word; each syllable keeps its full tone.

example.english: I like Taiwan more and more.

note: Sounds written or poetic. In speech people say 漂亮 piào liang or 好美 hǎo měi.

example.pinyin: Táiwān shì ge měilì de dìfāng.
Néng rènshi nǐ, wǒ hěn xìngyùn.

note: In Taiwan the normal word for a girl or woman of any age up to middle age, not just a schoolgirl; its pair is 男生 nán shēng 'guy'. Mainland 姑娘 is rarely heard.
Taiwan word; the mainland says 網絡 wǎng luò. 上網 shàng wǎng 'to go online'.

example.english: The internet at home is so slow.

hint: the whole leg, not the foot
note: 腳 jiǎo is 'foot', though Taiwanese often say 腳 for the leg too. Counted with 條 tiáo or 雙 shuāng.

example.pinyin: Pǎowán bù, wǒ de tuǐ hǎo tòng.
example.english: My legs really hurt after running.

note: 處 is chù 'place' here; in 處理 'to handle' it is chǔ.

example.english: I was just looking everywhere for you!

note: Experience as know-how. For events you lived through, 經歷 jīng lì is used.

example.pinyin: Nǐ yǒu kāichē de jīngyàn ma?
example.english: Do you have any driving experience?

note: Also used before a verb to mean 'officially': 正式開始 'officially start'.
A slightly more formal 'enough'. In everyday speech plain 夠 gòu is more common: 錢不夠 'not enough money'.
To have surgery is 動手術 dòng shǒu shù, or in casual Taiwan speech 開刀 kāi dāo.

example.trad: 我爸爸下個月要動手術。
example.simp: 我爸爸下个月要动手术。
example.pinyin: Wǒ bàba xià ge yuè yào dòng shǒushù.
example.english: My dad is having surgery next month.

example.pinyin: Zhè shì sòng nǐ de lǐwù.
example.english: This is a gift for you.

note: Also means going after someone romantically: 追女生 'to court a girl'. Also used for following a TV series: 追劇. The rare literary reading duī means 'to carve'.

example.pinyin: Tā zhuī le tā liǎng nián.
example.english: He pursued her for two years.

note: Taiwan (MOE) says tóu fǎ with a full third tone. Mainland speech says tóu fa.
Counts large, fixed things: 一座山, 一座橋, 一座廟. Buildings are usually counted with 棟 dòng in Taiwan. 'Seat' is 座位 zuò wèi.

hint: can follow a time word, like tomorrow
note: Usually in the pattern 就要…了 'about to happen'. Unlike 快要, it can follow a time word: 明天就要走了 'leaving tomorrow already'. Can also mean 'just want': 我就要這個.

example.english: The movie is about to start.

note: As a reply it means 'whatever, anything is fine'. Said of a person it means careless or sloppy: 他做事很隨便.
不 + 會: 'will not' (他不會來 'he won't come') or 'can't, never learned' (我不會游泳). In Taiwan it is also the usual reply to 謝謝: 'no problem'. 不 is spoken bú before huì.

example.pinyin: Fàngxīn, tā bù huì shēngqì de.
example.english: Don't worry, he won't be angry.

note: A body movement or gesture. In Taiwan 動作快一點 is a common way to say 'hurry up'.

example.pinyin: Tā de shēntǐ huīfù de hěn hǎo.

note: A general, slightly formal word. In casual speech people often say 吃的 chī de or 東西.
Counted with 隻 zhī: 一隻貓.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu liǎng zhī māo.
example.english: We have two cats at home.

gloss: quite a lot; quite a few
note: An understated 'a lot', literally 'not few'. 不 keeps its 4th tone here because 少 is a 3rd tone.

example.english: There are quite a few people today.

note: Most often an exclamation when something goes wrong. It can also describe a situation: 很糟糕 'really bad'.

example.pinyin: Zāogāo, wǒ wàng le dài yàoshi!
example.english: Oh no, I forgot my keys!

note: 恐怖片 is a horror movie. Taiwanese also use it loosely for anything awful: 好恐怖 'that's horrible'. Close to 可怕.

example.english: I'm too scared to watch horror movies.

note: Before a verb it means 'for nothing': 白跑一趟 'a wasted trip'. The color is usually said 白色 bái sè. MOE also lists a literary reading bó.

example.pinyin: Tā de tóufǎ dōu bái le.
example.english: His hair has all turned white.

note: A slightly more formal 更 gèng. In everyday speech plain 更 is more common.

example.pinyin: Tā biàn de gèngjiā nǔlì le.
